items.abstract: Moving beyond economic analyses of degrowth, growth and consumption are reframed through decomposition as a vital process through which life, value, and politics are continually re-composed. Against dominant imaginaries that cast decay as waste or ruination, this article turns to composting and carrion ecologies to articulate decomposition as a generative undoing and a mode of transformation that binds waste to worth. Drawing on multispecies examples from vultures in India to the Baltimore Compost Collective, the article situates decomposition as both material process and political metaphor to enact a revaluation of growth, decay, and consumption that unsettles capitalist logics of extraction and accumulation. It traces how practices of decay can cultivate livability and collective flourishing in the very sites marked by abandonment and disgust. In doing so, it challenges growth’s moral hegemony, recasts the ‘de-’ of decline, decay, and decomposition as a source of ecological vitality, and re-embeds growth within more-than-human cycles of breakdown and flourishing.
items.title: Rethinking (De)growth: the politics of compost

AI appears as a key theme in existential risk circles, not only as a source of risk, but also as a resource for risk prevention and as the enabler of a glorious future for humanity. However, what is it about AI that brings together utopian and dystopian imaginaries? Why is a discourse on AI so tied to questions regarding the human, and what forms of humanity does it produce? items.abstract: Scholars have read Leo Strauss’s Thoughts on Machiavelli (1958) as a theological-political treatise that offers timeless truths about politics. This article argues that it also aimed to convince American conservatives to embrace a muscular foreign policy. Strauss’s correspondence and seminar transcripts reveal that he wanted the United States to support embattled outposts of Western civilization and blamed Kant’s philosophy of history for enabling the rise of Nazism and communism. Thoughts on Machiavelli teaches American elites that politics often involves a choice among evils, strong leaders are necessary to found states, democracies are better than dictatorships at maintaining states, and propaganda can mobilize a multitude to join one’s army. The article shows that Strauss wanted to influence US policy regarding the State of Israel, Cuba, and Vietnam and deserves his reputation as the founder of neoconservatism.
items.title: “M. and the USA”: The Political Teaching of Leo Strauss’s Thoughts on Machiavelli

items.abstract: Arthur Schopenhauer’s philosophy has been systematically excluded from the canon of radical political thought, dismissed as quietist resignation incompatible with emancipatory projects. This article challenges that exclusion by developing the concept of the pluriversal subject, a political subjectivity derived from Schopenhauer’s metaphysics of will, ethics of compassion (Mitleid), and aesthetic cognition. Where Laclau’s empty signifier demands that particular claims be made equivalent—sacrificing irreducible difference at the moment of articulation—and Žižek’s neo-Hegelian framework reinstates a privileged subject-position grounded in class antagonism, the pluriversal subject achieves solidarity through compassionate recognition of shared suffering without homogenizing the plurality of political claims. Drawing on Schopenhauer’s epistemological break from the Kantian-Hegelian tradition, his engagement with non-Western philosophical traditions, the activation of his ideas through the Nietzschean-Deleuzian lineage and Latin American decolonial thought (Mignolo, Quijano), the article demonstrates that his metaphysics furnishes a non-rationalist, non-identitarian ground for radical de
items.title: Schopenhauer, Compassion, and the Radical Political Subject

items.abstract: Positional blurring is a common and effective party strategy. It enables parties to downplay some issues while highlighting and clarifying their profile on others. However, we know little about how parties use this strategy outside European party systems, in which (right-wing) populist parties are particularly noteworthy for their blurred economic positions and clear cultural positions. Is that strategy inherent to populism or a reflection of context-specific incentives? This article uses data from Europe and Latin America to argue that populists tailor their strategies to the dimensionality of their party system and populism’s host ideology. We find that multidimensional party systems and exclusionary thick ideologies drive populists to blur their economic positions. Extending this research field beyond Europe for the first time, these findings show that populists are heterogeneous actors whose varied thick ideologies embedded in diverse political systems systematically constrain their strategic behavior.
items.title: Positional Blurring in Context: How Dimensionality and Ideology Constrain Strategy

items.abstract: Thomas Paine is widely known for galvanizing public opinion in favor of the cause of American independence; his trenchant critique of Edmund Burke and spirited affirmation of the “rights of man”; and his contribution to the development of republicanism during constitutional debates in France. Yet there has been less scholarly attention to what is arguably Paine’s greatest revolution: namely, his vision of the United States as a “civic nation” whose membership is determined by consent to shared republican principles. A closer examination of Paine’s life and political writings reveals the strengths as well as the weaknesses of this civic ideal.
items.title: Thomas Paine’s Greatest Revolution: Nationality, Citizenship, and Civic Identity in America

items.abstract: This article examines contemporary digital governance through a dialogue between Shoshana Zuboff's theory of surveillance capitalism and Michel Foucault's analysis of power and governmentality. Although Zuboff offers a compelling account of the economic logics underlying digital domination, her framework tends to locate resistance primarily in external regulation and legal reform. This article argues that such an approach overlooks the subjectifying effects through which digital governance shapes compliant and predictable subjects. Drawing on Foucault, it reconceptualizes surveillance capitalism as an intensification of existing governmental rationalities and advances the notion of counter‐conduct to analyze how subjects negotiate and resist digital power from within.
items.title: Surveillance Capitalism and Governmentality Foucault in the Age of Digitization

items.abstract: Recent philosophers of secularization have given religion a more central place in their thinking about secular modernity and liberal democracy. This article argues that such theories have overlooked an important dimension of the contemporary social and political landscape, namely how the framework of separating ‘religious’ and ‘secular’ spheres can paradoxically affirm the hegemonic position of Christianity and marginalize non-Christian minorities. Drawing on the work of Gil Anidjar, the article instead develops a critical narrative of secularization which points to continuations of Christian hegemony in the ‘secular’ realm, despite and through the religion-secular binary. Bringing this to the forefront is crucial for understanding how secularism can be compatible with the rise in Christian nationalist politics in Europe and North America, as well as the marginalization of racial and religious minorities. Moreover, the article argues, rethinking secularization raises important new questions for normative theory about religion and politics.
items.title: Rethinking Secularization: The Religion-Secular Binary, Christianity, and the Politics of Exclusion

items.abstract: This article examines power and resistance in Margaret Atwood’s MaddAddam trilogy through the lens of Foucauldian biopolitics. Combining close textual analysis with political theory and literary studies, it argues that Atwood’s speculative fiction offers a powerful critique of contemporary capitalism by showing how life, bodies, and conduct become sites of government within neoliberal market logics. Set in a corporate-dominated world shaped by biotechnology and the commodification of public services, the trilogy shows that power operates not only through the management of bodies but also through the formation of subjects, encouraging individuals to treat themselves as projects to be managed, improved, and made valuable. Within and against this subject formation, resistance emerges through partial and fragile practices, taking the form of ethical practices, disruptive interventions, and refusals of the identities the regime seeks to impose. These forms of resistance show how the trilogy critiques contemporary power relations while envisioning alternatives grounded in care, community, and interdependence.
items.title: Power and Resistance in Margaret Atwood’s MaddAddam Trilogy

items.abstract: Normative political theorists typically view displacement as a phenomenon that entails forced movement. In this article, I challenge this orthodoxy by arguing that displacement is fundamentally a loss of one's place and/or home that may occur either with or without such movement. items.abstract: Nick Land is a British philosopher who has been leading the Dark Enlightenment movement. This paper examines the philosophical foundations of Land's right-wing trajectory and asks how the digital is integrated into his political economy and anti-humanist worldview. It situates Land within a broader context in which contemporary crises of neoliberal capitalism coincide with authoritarian and neo-reactionary currents often grouped under the label ‘Dark Enlightenment’. The analysis reconstructs continuities between Land's early work and his post-2013 writings by identifying five characteristic motifs that constitute the TOXIC schema, a mnemonic for the five key features of Nick Land's thought: T, the termination of Kant's influence; O, opposition to universalism and humanism; X, xeno-capitalism; I, informatic transhumanism; C, capitalist accelerationism. items.abstract: Understanding how voters use the left-right scale is essential, as it is not only related to vote choice but also underpins how political scientists study ideology. This article finds that the way voters use the left-right scale is variable. Using British Election Study Internet Panel data from 2014 to 2024, I find that while economic and cultural values are both related to left-right self-placement, this varies both between individuals and over time. Those on the left of the self-placement scale can best be differentiated from one another by the strength of their economic values. For those on the right, cultural values are more useful in separating between different self-placement levels. Over time, left-right self-placement has become increasingly related to cultural values alongside economic values, driven by movements by people on both sides of the left-right scale. These findings indicate that even within one country, the meanings of ‘left’ and ‘right’ vary.
items.title: The changing meaning of left-right self-placement in the United Kingdom

items.abstract: Critics of neoliberalism increasingly examine its corrosive effects on democracy. Scholars often turn to Friedrich Hayek's political theory, arguing that it produces citizens who passively conform to spontaneous social orders. Yet insufficient attention has been paid to the normative conception of the human individual underlying his neoliberalism. This article demonstrates that Hayek's theory actively rejects individuality, understood as the cultivation and expression of one's distinct personal character. Individuality requires an experimental approach toward social action and critical reflection on whether social rules express one's character, yet such attitudes are systematically stifled in Hayek's account because they threaten the unequivocal obedience his spontaneous orders demand. My reading suggests that by suppressing individuality in favor of unreflective conformity, Hayek's neoliberalism produces citizens who are particularly ill‐equipped to identify and resist threats to their freedom and sustain liberal democracy.
items.title: Individualism Without Individuality: Friedrich Hayek and the Neoliberal Citizen

items.abstract: Social theorists in the Marxian tradition often interpret philosophical problems as reflections of social problems. This approach is central to Adorno's interpretation of Kant's epistemology. Adorno claims that the Critique of Pure Reason develops a concept of subjectivity that mirrors the “functionalization” of experience in capitalist societies. He retains that concept contradictory just as the social functionalism it ideologically reflects. In this paper I argue that Kant's concept of subjectivity is not contradictory and that Adorno must rely on it to articulate his critique of functionalism. Recognizing this Kantian debt implies not just acknowledging the Kantian sources of Adorno's model of ideology critique, but also revising central aspects of his social theory.
items.title: Adorno and the Kantian Sources of Ideology Critique

items.abstract: For the American Fourierist movement known as Associationism, the European revolutions of 1848 represented the opening scene of a new world-historical struggle: “the Emancipation of Labor.” The momentous example of the French Revolution in particular pushed this group of cooperative labor reformers, often dismissed as “utopians,” to embrace the politics and persuasiveness of working-class agitation as a tactical means to reorganize the system of industry. I argue that the Associationists—sidelined, when not forgotten, in the existing scholarship of “the American 1848”—should be appreciated for placing socialism on the agenda as the promise of a future workers’ democracy in the United States. Not only that, but they came to view the US labor movement itself as a participant in the social and political transformations of the 1848 revolutions. This is the Associationist 1848.
items.title: The Associationist 1848 and the Promise of Socialism

items.abstract: Does exposure to conflict displacement amplify support for far-right parties? This study investigates the political consequences of conflict-induced displacement in northern Israel by exploiting a natural experiment arising from government-ordered evacuations during military conflicts. Using a pre-registered survey and a regression discontinuity design based on an exogenous 5 km threshold, I assess changes in retrospective and prospective voting behavior as well as self-reported political ideology. The analysis reveals no evidence that displacement increases far-right support or induces partisan realignment. Rather, evacuees demonstrate a modest rightward shift in ideological self-placement without corresponding changes in voting behavior. This divergence suggests that displacement influences symbolic political positioning without prompting corresponding changes in voting behavior. These patterns unfold against a broader backdrop of political frustration and electoral disengagement that affects both displaced and non-displaced populations. items.title: Shifting sands? The impact of conflict displacement on voting

items.abstract: This essay is a response to David Lay Williams’ reading of Plato’s political thought, in his book The Greatest of All Plagues: How Economic Inequality Shaped Political Thought from Plato to Marx . The review essay asks three questions: Does Williams see among practitioners of contemporary political thinking any sign of a return to the deeper moral and philosophical aspects of political theory and any sign of a move toward expanding on the safer statistical approaches he himself diagnoses as insufficient? Of the two modes of responding to radical inequality, the imposition of practical impediments to acquiring massive wealth versus the re-education of the population toward an attitude that does not value the excessive accumulation of wealth, does Williams see across the canon of thinkers he treats here any general preference for one over the other? And lastly, in response to Plato’s apparent observation of a tendency in human life to lose sight of the whole of the political community one exists in and to focus on smaller horizons of concern, are there any strategies in Plato or in the other thinkers he treats, that Williams would suggest are valuable in combatting this tendency?
items.title: On Williams on Plato

items.abstract: This article challenges the reduction of blockchain to an institutional technology for lowering transaction costs by interpreting it as an autopoietic system of operational closure. Drawing on Francisco Varela's theory of biological autonomy and Cornelius Castoriadis’ account of political autonomy, it distinguishes between functional autonomy, understood as systemic self-maintenance, and political autonomy, understood as collective self-institution. The article argues that blockchain governance is marked by a rigidity paradox: the deterministic mechanisms that secure trustless coordination also risk foreclosing the indeterminacy required for democratic deliberation. Through the cases of the Ethereum hard fork and KONG Land, the article shows how algorithmic consensus can produce a form of functional sovereignty while displacing the interpretive and instituting dimensions of law. It concludes by proposing the need to rethink decentralized governance as an open rather than closed autopoiesis.
items.title: Algorithmic autopoiesis and the operational closure of law: The performativity of consensus as the production of socio-political reality

items.abstract: This article traces a single, three-stage argument. It begins by documenting, with empirical precision, how digital platforms functioned as genuine instruments of horizontal mobilization during the North African uprisings of 2010–2012. It then analyses how those same platforms were rapidly incorporated into new and frequently more sophisticated architectures of social control, transforming what had been emancipatory tools into what Foucault would call dispositifs of docility. Finally, it asks what theoretical apparatus is adequate to comprehend this transition—and argues that the most productive framework is a deliberate synthesis of Foucault’s analytics of biopower and disciplinary normalization with Bauman’s diagnosis of liquid modernity. The contribution of Bauman is not merely decorative: his account of how solid disciplinary confinement mutates under liquid conditions into consensual, self-administered surveillance explains precisely why the digital panopticon is so much more difficult to resist than its institutional predecessors. items.abstract: Contemporary critical theory elevates social norms to the status of positive knowledge and proclaims a politics of normative rightness to realise positive freedom and material equality in capitalist society. By accepting the positivity of norms, it fetishises them and prevents their denunciation, which alone exposes them. Based on the critical theories of Marx and Adorno, the article examines social norms as norms of a historically specific social content. In this process, the freedom of form is exposed in its content as the ‘freedom to starve’ (Adorno). Critique of exploitation does not call for normative arguments to understand its normative deficiencies with a view to achieving improvements. To understand the social norms, one must think in and through them to grasp their secret in the freedom of labour, which is the freedom of needy individuals to secure wage income. The circumstance that their prospects depend on the profitability of their labour connects the (promise of) freedom with exploitation.
items.title: Normative values and social critique: On Adorno and Marx

items.abstract: Neal Harris's Critical Theory and the Critique of Alternative Societies represents a significant contribution to the revival of first-generation Frankfurt School critical theory and its application to the contemporary alternative societies movement. This review essay evaluates Harris's central argument – that experimental pluralism among alternative societies is undermined by insufficient critique and an actionist displacement of strategic thinking – by placing it in dialogue with the existing scholarship on real utopias, workers’ cooperatives, mutual aid and universal basic income. The essay affirms the explanatory power of Harris's Frankfurt School framework, particularly his deployment of reification, instrumental rationality and repressive desublimation, while raising critical questions about the scope of the analysis, the tension between negativity and praxis and the risk of reproducing a specifically Western, male-centred theoretical horizon. The review ultimately endorses Harris's call for a renewed synthesis of critique and activism as an urgent priority for critical social theory.

items.abstract: Contemporary diagnoses of resurgent authoritarianism frequently attribute it to the political mobilization of fear, drawing on a long tradition that casts fear as the antithesis of freedom. This article argues that such a framework is conceptually inadequate in the face of climate breakdown. It critically engages scholarship that cautions against environmental fear and catastrophist discourse, identifying three key assumptions underpinning most of these critiques: that environmental fears are politically homologous to other historically theorized forms of fear; that fear directly fosters authoritarian tendencies at the individual level; and that fear consolidates reactionary power while weakening emancipatory movements at the collective level. Against this affective determinism and threat functionalism, the article draws on ecofeminist and anti-militarist thought to reconceptualize fear not as a regressive affect opposed to democratic agency, but as an ambivalent, critical orientation toward shared vulnerability. items.title: Reclaiming Fear in the Age of Climate Breakdown: From the Biopolitics of Catastrophe to Affective Self-Defense

items.abstract: This paper addresses the problem of sexual misrecognition: some groups are excluded from being seen as sexually desirable or are hypersexualised. This shapes their sexual subjectivity – how they understand themselves as sexual agents. Despite widespread initiatives calling for recognition in the domain of sexuality, the need for sexual recognition has remained undertheorised in recognition theory. Building on debates on the ambivalence of recognition, I argue that sexuality has a uniquely complex relationship to recognition. While sexual recognition is necessary for subjectivity, it also reinforces subjection to power structures. Moreover, sexuality continually transgresses sociality and subjectivity itself. Using Jeanette Chedda’s erotic story in Damn Horny as a case study, I demonstrate how sexual recognition transgresses ideals of mutuality and equality, and theorise transformative possibilities for cultivating sexual subjectivity differently.
items.title: The Ambivalence of Recognition in Sexual Subjectivity

items.abstract: This article offers a systematic and critical analysis of ordoliberal engagements with nature. Drawing on published and unpublished writings, private correspondence, and public addresses of key ordoliberal thinkers, primarily Alexander Rüstow and Wilhelm Röpke, it argues that their environmental thought was neither a precocious ecological awareness nor a coherent policy program, but rather a deeply romantic and conservative cultural critique of modern industrial society. Situating ordoliberalism within the broader intellectual milieu of Lebensphilosophie and the Conservative Revolution, the article traces how environmental ideas were embedded within their civilizational critique of modernity, functioning as a normative benchmark for social and cultural order. It further demonstrates how their conception of nature served to naturalize social hierarchy and legitimize a parochial vision of small-scale, locally embedded communities that proved increasingly difficult to reconcile with the economic realities they simultaneously promoted.
items.title: “Idyllischer Gartenzwergkapitalismus”: A Distinct Ordoliberal Environmental Framework?

items.abstract: This article critically explores council democracy as a utopian state order, on the basis of anarchist and Marxist works from western Europe and the United States, post-World War 2. As a system of national government, council democracy cannot possibly deliver on its utopian promises. Collective self-rule cannot put an end to domination/hierarchy/rule but will engender another variety of ‘democratic hierarchy’. Comprehensive citizen participation locks citizens in an overregulated ‘democratic bureaucracy’, and delivers no feasible, working formula of government. In a paradox, council democracy is likely greatly to reduce the share of the population participating in the country’s political process, thus carrying less rather than more democratic legitimacy than representative democracy.
items.title: Collective Self-Rule and Comprehensive Participation: A Critique of Council Democracy

items.abstract: According to Adorno, all attempts to change society “immediately come up against the overwhelming force of inertia in the prevailing situation, and seem condemned to impotence.” This article explores the way the phenomenon of social and institutional inertia has been addressed in recent Critical Theory. It poses two central questions: firstly, what is social inertia, and what causes it? And secondly, how do we judge when institutions or social norms are “inert” or “obsolete”? It first briefly discusses the historical background of the problem of inertia, obsolescence and second nature in Hegel, Marx and the first generation of the Frankfurt School, and then discusses the central questions primarily with reference to recent work by Jaeggi and Menke and, to a lesser extent, Rosa and Von Redecker.
items.title: Social Inertia in Critical Theory

items.abstract: This review essay critically engages Andrew Hartman's Karl Marx in America , a reception history of three different classes of readings of Marx's writings in the United States. The essay's main contention is that Hartman's text, however unintentionally, seems to deviate from and thus challenges the anti-foundational principles that orient the genre of reception history. For, echoing Shakespeare's, Hegel's, and Marx's uses of the metaphor of the “Old Mole,” Hartman's own commitment to a labor-oriented version of “Marx”—from the three he charts in his topography of the Marx–America dialectic—works its way through Karl Marx in America , appearing at the end of text to subvert the groundless doctrines that guide reception histories.
items.title: “Well grubbed, old mole!”: On Karl Marx in America by Andrew Hartman, University of Chicago Press, 2025

items.abstract: This article examines how sustainability is rendered publicly legitimate in the current phase of green capitalism. Rather than treating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) as mere ideology or Solarpunk as external critique, it approaches both as modalities of public testing within a shared moral field. Drawing on Boltanski and Thévenot's sociology of justification, it argues that ecological legitimacy today is structured by a dominant normative test embedded in ESG discourse and a subordinate yet consequential sensible test, in which sustainability must also appear credible within shared perceptual horizons. To conceptualize this second dimension, the article introduces the notion of épreuve de sensibilité : a public test of rightness operating on the affective and aesthetic plane. Through a comparative analysis of European ESG regulatory texts (2019–2025) and a multilingual corpus of Solarpunk narratives (2012–2024), it shows how ecological morality is stabilized as procedural coherence in governance and staged as perceptual consonance in cultural imaginaries
items.title: Captured by the sun? Solarpunk, environmental, social, and governance criteria, and the pragmatics of green justification

items.abstract: In this text I reconstruct the thinking behind Althusser’s work to define philosophy, which culminated in his 1976 presentation at the Granada conference. I start by exploring how philosophy exploits and reorganises other forms of knowledge and social practices by means of an analysis of Althusser’s works in the later part of the 1960s. Subsequently, I examine and outline the debates on how the mode of production affects the superstructure. I then turn to the positions of Althusser’s interlocutor at the Granada conference, Juan Carlos Rodríguez, who defended the idea that philosophy was affected by the mode of production. Finally, I examine the implications of the changes and innovations in Althusserian thought set out at the conference for the conception of philosophy.
items.title: The Althusserian Transformation of Philosophy

items.abstract: Drawing on Heller’s sustained dialogue with Kant and Marx, the paper argues for the continuing relevance of her social philosophy while also foregrounding unexpected affinities between these two classic figures in their respective conceptions of social and political community. I first examine Heller’s interpretation of the Marxian ethical-political legacy, paying particular attention to social experiments such as the Paris Commune and their significance for a radical Enlightenment project that rethinks the relationship between state and society. I then inspect Heller’s engagement with Kant and Marx on the historical continuity of republicanism, highlighting the rejection of instrumental domination and the demand for symmetric reciprocity among social agents. Finally, I analyze Heller’s theory of needs, particularly the concept of “radical needs,” and argue for its relevance to contemporary debates on democracy, social reproduction and non-paternalistic forms of political organization.
items.title: From Marx to Kant: Social Domination and Emancipatory Praxis in Ágnes Heller

items.abstract: This article undertakes a historical-critical investigation of the intertwining of critical theory and functionalism in steps. It takes Adorno's critique of functionalism in architecture as a point of departure to distinguish the specific sense in which ‘functionalism’ is defined and subsequently rejected. The following section scrutinizes how critical theory deploys functionalist explanation, consciously or unconsciously, as the operative dynamic of its social diagnosis. On this basis, the third section utilises previously articulated methodological distinctions to outline critical theory's attempts at a normative reconstruction of the category of ‘function’. Then the inquiry pivots to the debates within analytical Marxism to examine critical theory's over-reliance on ‘objective teleology’ within its social diagnosis. Finally, the paper returns to the primary texts of sociological functionalism to refute critical theory's stereotype that equates function with end, thereby recovering more sophisticated understandings of functionalism for sociological analysis.
items.title: ‘Functionalist prejudice’: Critical theory and teleology

items.abstract: This article reevaluates Walling as a neglected precursor to American Western Marxism, arguing that his 1912–1914 trilogy synthesized Marxist theory of his time and Deweyan pragmatism into a distinct “pragmatist conception of history.” Born into “aristocracy” yet radicalized, Walling's unique trajectory—as a co‐founder of the NAACP and critic of Second International orthodoxy—shaped his approach: a rejection of deterministic scientific history in favor of instrumental, presentist analysis limited to recent generations. Although his work anticipated Western Marxism's cultural turn and superstructural focus, it also embodied tensions between materialist foundations and pragmatist subjectivity. Through critical engagement with Walling's contradictions—his Deweyan compromise, Nietzschean anti‐historicism, and idealist leanings—the article reveals the limits of his project. Ultimately, Walling's legacy lies in his paradoxical role: a bridge between Second International economism and later Marxist humanism, whose flaws illuminate broader challenges in adapting Marxism and its readings.
items.title: William E. Walling and the Pragmatist Foundations of Proto‐Western Marxism: A Re‐Evaluation and Critique

items.abstract: This essay explores the distinctive humanist method through which The Greatest of All Plagues investigates the presence of economic inequality in the history of political thought. It then follows the various thinkers in the book—from Plato to Marx—and observes that a vocabulary of virtue and wisdom not only accompanies but often underwrites criticisms of inequality deep into the 19th century. In conclusion, Williams’ book implicitly allows his readers to perceive how virtue ethics and criticisms of inequality have only become separated in the late modern period. In the 21st century, their rapprochement will deepen and energize inquiries into virtue ethics and egalitarian approaches to political economy alike.
items.title: Virtue, wisdom, and inequality: A response to David Lay Williams’ The Greatest of All Plagues

items.abstract: If Foucault was anything, he was a particularist. And yet, if we are to find valuable tools in his method today, they must be able to assist our framing and analysis of non‐particular issues. By what means can Foucault's methods grasp trans‐contextual problems? I investigate this question by reconsidering the status of power in Foucault's genealogical method. Rather than acting as an object of inquiry, I propose that power operates as an orienting analytical category at the level of Foucault's method. I make the case that conceiving of power in this way facilitates a substantial degree of generalization of his approach that he and his commentators have frequently been wary of claiming. This rethinking of power and method establishes the capacity for Foucaultian methods to address contemporary systemic and global problems.
items.title: The Purview of the Particular: Power and Method in Foucaultian Genealogy

items.abstract: : Using speculative fiction as a cultural probe, this essay critiques “deathbots” as extensions of late neoliberal capitalism. By examining Black Mirror , Upload , and The Final Cut , I make the case that these stories demonstrate a colonization of grief where the dead become extractable data for profit and the bereaved become dependent users. The essay draws on Homi Bhabha’s concept of mimicry and Sherry Turkle’s “ELIZA effect” to show how artificial intelligence simulacra trap mourners in loops of sycophantic affirmation that interfere with real grief. These technologies, I argue, foster a “crisis of narration,” the inability to achieve the temporal closure necessary to mark an end to grief and transform the raw data of loss into shared meaning. Ultimately, digital afterlives foster emotional stasis rather than healing, necessitating a critical recovery of memory and communal rituals in an era of algorithmic intimacy.
items.title: Digital Necromancy and the Fictional Imaginary: Speculative Probes into Deathbots and the Neoliberal Afterlife

items.abstract: This introduction to the special issue “What is Sedimentation? Consciousness, History, Language” clarifies the central role of sedimentation in Husserlian and post-Husserlian phenomenology and sets the stage for the essays that follow. Borrowed from geology, sedimentation functions in phenomenology as a concept-metaphor for the temporal layering of experience, habit, and meaning, linking static, genetic, and generative phenomenology. It names both the formation of a sedimented unconscious and the possibility of reactivation, thereby grounding phenomenological accounts of historicity, tradition, and critique. The introduction focuses on Husserl, Merleau-Ponty, Ricœur, Gadamer, and Derrida, while also indicating later reinterpretations in figures such as Stiegler and in political theory. It then presents the individual contributions, which explore sedimentation across embodiment, language, narrative, institutions, surprise, gesture, and psychopathology, showing how it conditions continuity while opening possibilities of transformation.
items.title: What is sedimentation?

items.abstract: Factionalism broadly describes the occurrence of conflicts between varying groups (or factions) within a social movement. Factionalism is often thought to be a negative feature of social movements. The goal of this paper is to (a) motivate the significance of the concept of factionalism for social and political philosophy and (b) give a definition of factionalism that captures the sense in which factionalism is a deep political problem. Specifically, the paper argues that factionalism is a form of anti-solidarity; factional groups are groups that, in virtue of their normal functionings, promote anti-solidaristic relations. Consequently, factionalism is particularly harmful because it has a transformative effect on movement actors: namely, it creates actors who are unwilling or unable to engage in collective political struggle. In a slogan: factionalism atomizes.
items.title: What Is Factionalism?

items.abstract: This response to critics addresses the questions raised throughout the symposium on the various issues raised throughout the Greatest of All Plagues . I address some of Cordelli's concerns about Hobbes's empirical assumptions by turning to Tocqueville. I answer Kirkland's questions regarding the nature of reforms intended to rectify inequality—whether practical or moral. Finally, I address Arlen's objections that the book has focused too much on the moral dimensions of inequality at the possible cost of underemphasizing the dangers of oligarchy. This particular concern provides an opportunity to discuss Walzer's Spheres of Justice and the difficulties of walling off inequality from other spheres of social life.
items.title: Response to critics

items.abstract: Social media and the internet have created new ways for representatives to communicate. How have members of Congress responded to these opportunities? We introduce a multi-platform dataset of congressional communications extending back to the onset of the social media era. Using computational language processing, we classify approximately 4.7 million tweets, 2.4 million Facebook posts, and 184,000 email newsletters authored by members of Congress between 2009 and 2022 based on intended purpose, and scale the partisanship of each message along a continuous left–right dimension. After validation, we demonstrate how our data can be used to study partisanship and representation in the contemporary Congress. Importantly, our data show congressional rhetoric has become more partisan and negative as social media usage has increased. We identify one potential mechanism contributing to this trend: partisanship and negativity receive inflated levels of positive engagement on social media relative to other forms of messaging like credit claiming or constituency service.
items.title: Measuring Partisanship and Representation in Online Congressional Communications

items.abstract: Jacob Taubes’s book Occidental Eschatology (1947) offers a unique framework for examining cultural patterns across the line often construed as separating ‘the religious’ from the ‘non-religious’. This article highlights the implications of the application of this framework for our understanding of modernity: With Taubes, the ‘modern’ conception of history, totality and sovereignty can be traced to the emphatic distinction between ‘world’ and ‘God’ in the Hebrew Bible. In this perspective, ‘the modern’ appears as a cultural element that is analytically dissociated from any particular later historical period and from any cultural or geographical context, such as ‘the West’. Messianic thinking appears integral to the modern rather than as a source of fundamentally opposing insights. Competing appeals to reject the world are a source of instability and violence in modernity. Further research can address how the modern is linked with other cultural elements and with institutional arrangements in different contexts.
items.title: Rethinking the Modern and Modernity with Jacob Taubes

items.abstract: This article critically examines the ongoing debate about whether the British Empire was a force for good, exemplified by the recent exchange between Robert Tombs and Alan Lester, as well as Nigel Biggar’s defence in Imperial Reckoning . It highlights how defenders of imperialism use historical narratives to justify colonial atrocities and resist critique. It argues that imperialism’s legacy persists through three main forms. (1) Structural power and domination: the colonial project established entrenched systems of political, military, and economic control, justified by narratives that portrayed the West as morally superior. (2) Historiography and glorification: imperial defenders construct dominant histories that glorify empire, marginalize dissent, and present their perspective as objective truth and, in the process, silence alternative voices. (3) Contemporary cultural reconfigurations: modern imperialism manifests in culture wars – attack on wokeism, targeted hostility towards LGBTQ+ communities, migrants, and other marginalized groups. items.abstract: Debates on catastrophic artificial intelligence (AI) risk often frame artificial superintelligence as a problem of value alignment: the central task is to ensure that advanced systems act in accordance with human intentions or moral principles. This article argues that such a framing is necessary but insufficient. The danger posed by artificial superintelligence is not merely that it may pursue the wrong values, but that it may introduce a new concentration of autonomous and potentially dominating power. Drawing on political realism in both political theory and international relations, we reinterpret AI catastrophic risk as a structural problem of power under anarchy. The core concerns of AI safety—instrumental convergence, race dynamics, and loss of control—already rely on implicitly realist assumptions about survival, self-help, and the pursuit of power. Yet proposed solutions often retreat into moralism, asking states, firms, or machines to behave ethically without sufficiently altering the incentives that drive competitive acceleration. Against both moralistic reassurance and fatalistic resignation, we argue that realism offers a constructive response. Fear can coordinate divid
items.title: Fear, power, and superintelligence: A realist reframing of AI catastrophic risk

items.abstract: This article offers a new reading of decadence in Nietzsche, not as a time of despair or sclerosis, but as one of individuality and freedom. It does so by focusing on decadence’s emancipatory potential for exceptional individuals. For Nietzsche, the best philosophers, artists, and heroes do not merely emerge despite, but thanks to, decadence. Decadent times come with the collapse of institutions, conventions, and values—a self-destructive milieu that proves catastrophic for the many, but offers the possibility of emancipation for the few. I then show that some of Nietzsche’s core concepts are tied to this account of decadence, and suggest that Nietzsche’s view can offer a counterpoint to competing accounts of decadence from reactionary critics of modernity.
items.title: Nietzsche on Decadence as Freedom

items.abstract: Disagreement about democracy's noninstrumental value often sees the opposition between two competing approaches. Liberty‐based arguments assign normative priority to a principle of liberty, thereby focusing on democratic self‐government as the core principle through which political authority can be reconciled with individual liberty. Equality‐based arguments fundamentally appeal to equality instead, thus commending democratic procedures for treating citizens as equals in the decision‐making process. This paper targets Thomas Christiano's public equality argument for democracy, showing that its tacit reliance on a noncomparative norm of respect for the free and autonomous person leads it back to the liberty framework, as traditionally understood.
items.title: The Contested Grounds of Democracy's Noninstrumental Value: Deliberative Democracy Versus Public Equality

items.abstract: Breaking carries many meanings, yet public life rarely lets it remain multiple: interruption is most often made legible only as damage awaiting repair. This article follows breaking through contemporary social movements to specify what a critical tradition descending from Foucault, Scott, and De Certeau leaves underarticulated, now that infrastructural systems are designed to anticipate and absorb disruption. Reading Alfred Sohn-Rethel’s account of Neapolitan tinkering, alongside Yuk Hui’s diagnosis of unbreakable technical ensembles, the argument situates breaking as world-making: a material politics over what is held together, what is relinquished, and at whose cost. Four contemporary repertoires – the No TAV movement, Soulèvements de la Terre , the looting of Black uprisings, and algorithmic poisoning – yield four recurring dimensions of breaking as intentionality, labour, temporality, and byproduction. Against repair’s moral economy, breaking emerges here as a diagnostic practice that prises open provisional futures where systems still give way.
items.title: Beyond Repair: Breaking as World-Making in Contemporary Social Movements

items.abstract: This article contributes to contemporary debates about racial capitalism by turning to Stuart Hall, a Jamaican cultural theorist active in the British New Left and the Birmingham Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies. Hall made two moves to better diagnose the mediating role that “race” and racism played in the crises of post-war British capitalism. First, he adopted an imperial frame that situated Britain's industrialization in relation to its colonial sites of production. Second, Hall developed a “Marxism without final guarantees” that could explain how racialized difference becomes embedded within relations of production as a regulative norm. I argue his approach should be preferred to both formal and world-historical theories of racial capitalism, as the latter can fall back into an oversimplified economism. Hall's conjunctural analysis, by contrast, makes space for a more sustained consideration of both (a) the state and (b) a materialist account of popular culture.
items.title: Toward a conjunctural critique of racial capitalism

items.abstract: With the initial publication of his main economic work in 1859, Marx formulated his programme for an analysis of the bourgeois economy in the following order: capital, landed property, wage labour; state, foreign trade, world market. It was not until the 1920s and 1950s that Henryk Grossman and Roman Rosdolsky discussed whether the content of ‘Capital’ was based on a change in Marx’s structural plan. Important impulses for this discussion in the GDR , the FRG and the Soviet Union came in the following years from the advancing publication of the MEGA ² since 1976. We pay particular attention to the work of Wolfgang Jahn’s research group at the University of Halle. At the heart of this was and is the question of whether methodological and/or substantive breaks can be recognised in Marx’s critique of political economy that point to a change in his conceptions of planning. We deny this with reference to the continuity of his dialectical method of antithetical determination.
items.title: Structure and Method of the Critique of Political Economy: On the Debate over Marx’s Structural Plan – Part One

items.abstract: Under neoliberalism, capitalist accumulation has become increasingly dependent on finance, including the financialisation of social reproduction. The centrality of finance to the reproduction of capital has been linked to both the global spread of informal and precarious forms of labour and the reconfiguration of state institutions according to the interests of finance capital. While the recomposition of capital, the working class, and the state has occurred unevenly, these processes have everywhere made the global working class more reliant on debt to ensure their own social reproduction, and these debt relations have become increasingly tied to the reproduction of finance capital. This paper demonstrates how, over the last several decades, intensified financialisation – defined as interest bearing capital ( IBC ) playing a key role in capitalist accumulation – has made both the reproduction of capital and the reproduction of the worker more dependent on finance, without displacing the pivotal role in accumulation played by value-producing wage labour.
items.title: Integrating Finance and Social Reproduction: Capital, Labour-Power, and Working-Class Formation

items.abstract: This essay intervenes in contemporary debates around neoliberalism and its relationship to both authoritarianism and social democracy. It does so by reconstructing the debate on Thatcherism that took place between Stuart Hall and Bob Jessop in the 1980s. Both authors provide materialist analyses of Thatcherism that point to important continuities, at the level of both political economy and authoritarian political technique, between her hegemonic project and late-stage social democracy. I argue that this provides an antidote to the social democratic nostalgia that is the potential product of the ways that neoliberalism is frequently theorised in the contemporary literature. While both thinkers highlight these continuities, they are more obviousin Jessop’s institutional approach to hegemony than in Hall’s analysis of Thatcher’s ideology.
items.title: The Origins of Neoliberal Authoritarianism: Hall and Jessop on the Crisis of Social Democracy and the Rise of Thatcher

items.abstract: Social experiences of unfairness resist standard distributional accounts. This article argues that comparative relations do not merely shape responses to unequal outcomes but participate in constituting the sense of entitlement through which those outcomes are experienced as unfair. items.abstract: What makes a body of work ‘canonical’? In his writings over the years Jeffrey C. Alexander offers some phenomenologically convincing answers, each suggesting that the power of canonical texts is simultaneously context-immanent and context-transcending. However, a critical theory of ‘the canon’ cannot confine itself to phenomenological description. A critical theory is necessary due to the social constitution of the meanings of canonical texts. This gives rise to an endemic risk of ideological biases and the danger that canonization will reproduce and reinforce dominant perceptions of intellectual value, excluding or marginalizing authors and works who do not fit well with these perceptions. Accordingly, theories cognizant of this risk must explain the context-transcending component of the normativity of canonical works in a non-reductive way. This is a challenge for critical sociology.
items.title: Criticizing ‘the canon:’ A challenge for cultural sociology

items.abstract: This article argues that democratic double standards are not episodes of normative inconsistency but a mutable political technology for the differential distribution of legitimacy. The concept names a historically changing ensemble of institutional apparatuses, justificatory rationalities and material infrastructures through which the threshold of democratic legitimacy is unevenly allocated while its political function persists. It is distinguished from organised hypocrisy, ideology and discourse by four features: a function/mechanism distinction, institutional materiality, genealogical temporality and colonial asymmetry. The argument unfolds through a theory-generating genealogy organised around the Chile–Brazil axis – a historically dense dyad that condenses the technology in unusually legible form. Three moments of mutation are reconstructed: anti-communist destabilisation in Chile, the regionalisation of repression through Operation Condor and the reorganisation of political antagonism in Brazil. Integrating governmentality and the coloniality of power, it approaches Latin America as a theoretical archive for theorising the unevenness of democratic universalism.
items.title: Democratic double standards as a mutable political technology: A historical genealogy from Latin America

items.abstract: This contribution explores power and solidarity in Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology, bringing together his reflections on the social world in Phenomenology of Perception with his appraisal of sociology and Marxism in Signs and Adventures of the Dialectic . I argue that Merleau-Ponty reconfigures power as the crystallization of social interest that connects individuals and groups despite the differences in their social and political membership. This paves the way for a reconsideration of solidarity as the power to institute a different sense of reality from the shared experience of work and oppression. I conclude with an illustration of the contingency of solidarity in connection with the social struggle that led to the Italian law 199/2016 against the exploitation of undocumented workers.
items.title: Power and solidarity in Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology

items.abstract: Louis Althusser shows how interpellation functions as a mechanism for the constituting of subjects delineated through ideology. While Althusser focuses his analysis on verbal interpellation, critical theorists have shown that interpellation need not be limited to vocative hails. In this article, I show how one can interpellate with their bodily motility, comportment, and even physiological functions. In particular, I argue that racist ideologies can become naturalized onto bodies in such a way that individuals can interpellate racialized others as inhabiting inferior social positions. Racist embodied interpellations call racialized subjects to see themselves occupying stereotypical images which can fundamentally impact identity shaping processes. However, it is not the case that this subject formation is ontologically totalizing. Rather, embodied interpellations can cause the hailed racialized subject to confront the conflict between their own self-image and the dominant stereotypical perception of them. items.abstract: This paper proposes a reconstruction of Sartre’s ontology of interpersonal relations organized around the concept of recognition. It begins with Honneth’s critique of Sartre, taking it as an opportunity to clarify the distinctive character of Sartre’s ontological approach to recognition. Central to this approach is the idea that a tension exists between intersubjective intimacy and existential separation, which Sartre regards as constitutive of the self-other relation. His analysis of this tension hinges on the concept of original recognition, as embodied in our affective response to the look of the Other. This recognition, however, is inherently ambiguous. While attesting to an original generosity of our interpersonal relations, it is also the source of potential conflict – a conflict that need not be perpetual but can be constructively overcome.
items.title: Sartre on the Ambiguity of Recognition

items.abstract: This paper examines Jacques Derrida’s and Gillian Rose’s conceptions of “home” as an ambiguous realm between belonging and estrangement, rootedness and displacement. Both resist simple accounts of home as a stable refuge or secure place of origin, yet they differ in how they respond to its incompleteness. For Derrida, home is shaped by fear of dissolution and loss—loss of belonging, collapse of the safety that makes dwelling possible. This fear gives home a “spectral” quality, visible in the aporetic structure of hospitality and in the terror of linguistic homelessness. Rose, drawing on Hegelian speculative identity, understands home as a process of mediation, formed through the ongoing work of negotiating contradictions in the present. Through readings of texts from the 1980s and 1990s, this paper argues that their different orientations toward fear and mediation yield distinct ethical and political visions. items.abstract: The present paper advances a reading of contemporary political apathy by rejecting its reduction to contingent sociological factors, and instead situating it within a transformation of the conditions of belief. Drawing on a Hegelian–Marxian lineage, it reinterprets the notion of Weltgeist as a secularized, ‘infra-material’ structure of shared intelligibility that conditions political participation. The argument contends that late capitalism has not merely commodified social relations but has attenuated the horizon within which belief acquires binding force, thereby producing a diffuse disaffection that manifests most acutely among younger cohorts in the ‘Western’ block. Against empiricist accounts of abstentionism, the paper proposes that disengagement is symptomatic of a deeper exhaustion of symbolic efficacy: political forms persist, but their capacity to command conviction has waned. items.abstract: What you are about to read is based on my work in progress called The Disparate: Deleuze’s Ethics of the Univocity of Being . My book attempts to extract a kind of ethics from the three theoretical books Deleuze published at the end of the Nineteen-Sixties: Expressionism in Philosophy: Spinoza (1968); Difference and Repetition (1968); and Logic of Sense (1969). Its widest aim lies in systematizing this ethics of the univocity of being. The first part of the article is theoretical. It concerns the ontology found in Difference and Repetition . The primary ontological concepts are those of the fold and multiplicity. The second part is practical. Here, I make a preliminary attempt to systematize the ethics of the univocity of being. Power is the hinge between the two parts, between the theory and the practice. For Deleuze, the meaning of being is power and the ethics of the univocity of being is an ethics of power. However, at the bottom of the ethics is the experience of powerlessness, even the experience of sadness. Only the experience of sadness puts one on the way to a beatific existence.
items.title: On the Way to a Beatific Existence: Theory and Practice in Deleuze’s Works at the End of the Nineteen-Sixties

items.abstract: This paper argues that longing for a departed beloved is neither a residual phase of grief nor a compensatory strategy, but a genuine mode of being-with-the-dead. It is ecstatically structured, affectively ambivalent, and grounded in the asymmetrical bond between the living and the dead. Drawing on Martin Heidegger’s notion of being-with and Jean-Luc Nancy’s essays “Psyche” and “On the Point of Departure,” I analyze the affective and temporal structure of longing through my recurring experience of my father’s withdrawal, more than a decade after his death. Nancy’s accounts of holding vigil and ecstatic resurrection allow me to articulate what Heidegger glimpsed but sidelined: the insistent pull of the departed as a withdrawal that continues to call upon those who remain. Longing is both cruel and serene: cruel because it exposes an unbridgeable distance, serene because it allows the departed to remain with us precisely in the exactitude of their withdrawal.
items.title: Longing: an Existential-Phenomenological Analysis of Being-With Our Beloved Departed

items.abstract: This paper treats anthropocentrism as a relational standing-order rather than only as a claim about intrinsic value. Anthropocentric arrangements give default priority to human convenience and self-image while shifting vulnerability and accountability costs elsewhere. The argument integrates moral deskilling, responsibility-gap analysis, relational standing, and vulnerability-first reasoning to explain a recurring pattern across nonhuman animals, environmental relations, and AI-mediated systems. Distorted relations damage intellectual capacities of understanding, judgment, and verification; emotional capacities of empathy, aversion, and attachment; and volitional capacities of commitment, responsibility-taking, and self-control. I analyze relational breakdown through instrumentalization, miscalibrated social response, responsibility diffusion, and attentional or empathic pollution. AI serves as an amplifier case because conversational, recommender, and automation systems can make these elements visible at scale. The paper proposes a minimal protocol: responsibility ownership, vulnerability-first attention, public anchors of traceability, contestability, and corrigibility, and capac
items.title: A Minimal Protocol for Right Relations: Reframing the Critique of Anthropocentrism Through Responsibility, Vulnerability, and Public Anchors

items.abstract: Small nations occupy an ambiguous position within modern political life: they are formally recognized political subjects, yet their historical experience is persistently shaped by exposure to external domination, geopolitical dependency, and the recurring possibility of rupture. Their political existence is thus marked not by stable continuity alone, but by a heightened sensitivity to vulnerability, contingency, and the threat of non-existence. Despite this, contemporary political theory has struggled to conceptualize small nations beyond descriptive accounts of nationalism or episodic disruptions of an otherwise stable political order. Drawing on Jan Patočka’s political phenomenology, this article reconceptualizes vulnerability as a constitutive and collective condition of political life. Rather than treating vulnerability as an anomaly to be overcome, it analyzes how exposure to historical rupture shapes political agency, responsibility, and solidarity. By interpreting small nations as exposed communities , the article shows how political meaning and judgment emerge under conditions in which continuity cannot be assumed and guarantees remain fragile. In doing so, it challenges do
items.title: Precarious Collectives: Rethinking Political Vulnerability Through Jan Patočka

items.abstract: What is Hobbes's attitude toward economic inequality, and should his sovereign pursue radical redistribution? In The Greatest of All Plagues, David Lay Williams argues that the Hobbesian sovereign must widely disperse wealth, since preserving peace under the laws of nature requires it, and concentrated wealth threatens that peace. This essay challenges that claim. First, drawing on Hobbes's distinction between just and good laws, I argue redistribution is not a duty of justice for the sovereign, only something a prudent sovereign would choose to do. Second, given the acquisitive character of Hobbesian felicity, and given that wealth is merely one form of social power among several, stability and peace may not always be best secured through radical redistribution. Finally, I reflect on the limits of using Hobbes to critique modern inequality, suggesting a paradox: the more extreme inequality becomes, the weaker the Hobbesian case for having a sovereign is in the first place.
items.title: Hobbes, inequality, and redistribution

items.abstract: In recent years, amidst the rise of authoritarianism and other injustices, political theorists are reevaluating the normative boundaries of political disobedience. This review compares and evaluates two recent contributions to this effort from Avia Pasternak and William E. Scheuerman. It identifies shared features such as the importance of democratic equality and the instrumental value of disobedience before explaining how they disagree about the concept and permissibility of violence. The review concludes that ultimately the fundamental divide between the authors is not whether citizens may ever use violence in defense of their basic rights and interests, but where and when the conditions obtain for permissibly doing so.
items.title: When, where, and how may citizens be violent?

items.abstract: This paper engages with recent debates about the value and future of work by proposing a shift in perspective: instead of asking whether work is normatively good or bad, the focus is placed on how work operates. Drawing on Michel Foucault’s concept of the dispositive, I conceptualise work as a historically specific and strategic arrangement of discourses, institutions, practices, and norms that binds individuals to the social world. Using Kathi Weeks’ theory of work’s antinomies, I show how contradiction is not incidental to work but central to its mode of operation. This framework makes it possible to reassess both contemporary attempts to recover the moral worth of work and post-work imaginaries that aim to abolish it. The paper argues that prominent normative accounts of work (e.g. Honneth, Gheaus and Herzog) overlook the mechanisms through which work is constituted as meaningful, while post-work theories, though politically generative, tend to underestimate the infrastructural and affective grip of the work dispositive. Reframing work as a dispositive thus offers a more critical and nuanced account of how it continues to shape subjectivity, social order, and ethical life—even i
items.title: How Work Works on Work as a Dispositive

items.abstract: This paper reconsiders the ‘working day’ discussion in chapter ten of Capital and how it centres two parameters in the generation and appropriation of surplus value. The first parameter is the cost of labour-power paid by the capitalist and the second is the time that the worker must yield to the capitalist: the ‘length of the working day’. The first parameter represents the amount of pay required to keep the worker alive and able to work. Marx understood it as a lower limit below which capitalism would cease to function. This paper argues that, while analytically coherent, this understanding of a lower limit runs contrary to many ways that actual historical capitalism has found to exploit the working class. Capitalism regularly exceeds this limit and, in this sense, hyper-exploits. What we find instead of a limit are racialised gradients of human value – generated and fostered by capitalism – in which there are regular and persisting areas of hyper-exploitation with devalued racialised gendered workers. Supplemented by the notion of gradients of human value, Marx’s two-parameter account with its unifying analytic of time, in particular human-time, neatly encompasses the phenomenon
items.title: Racialised Gradients of Human Value and Marx’s Working Day, Today

items.abstract: Despite its prominence in the history of political thought, the analogy between states and organisms has fallen into disrepute. Evolutionary theory, however, gives reason to reconsider it. The Price equation, a model drawn from theoretical biology, identifies specific conditions that facilitate the transition from a collection of individuals to a collective organism. It thereby provides a powerful framework for resolving the longstanding debate in political theory between those who view states as cohesive organisms and critics who emphasize rational individual choice. Our analysis suggests that organic theory can withstand the main criticisms offered by methodological individualists, but only with certain qualifications. Although organic theory is unlikely to apply to large, modern states, it may prove useful when applied to subnational entities.
items.title: From collection to collective: Institutional conditions for the organic state

items.abstract: Political theorists have long focused their understanding of democratic education on the institution of the school, particularly the public school, to the exclusion of broader visions of education beyond schooling. But as criticisms of schooling from outside the academy mount, it becomes imperative to examine the origins of American educational thought to determine whether opposition to schooling has an older historical source. This essay locates the roots of school skepticism in an alternative American educational tradition beginning with Benjamin Franklin that drew on Locke’s pedagogical arguments to devalue institutional schooling in favor of self-education. Franklin’s educational vision harnessed the independence of the young in early America by incentivizing learning through friendship and self-interest, and resorted to schools only as a guardrail against the abuse of freedom, incorporating them but minimizing their role in education. In this, Franklin initiated the Americanization of Lockean pedagogy, or the school-skeptical tradition in American thought.
items.title: Benjamin Franklin and Democratic Education Beyond Schooling

items.abstract: This article argues that the case of an idiosyncratic digital movement in Paris—#saccageparis—has much to contribute to recent debates around social media’s democratic potential. #saccageparis leaders paint themselves as contemporary tribunes of the plebs, a permanent counter-power representing the “small people” of Paris against the municipality. Based on ethnographic fieldwork, I examine in this article such claim. On the one hand, Twitter’s affordances enabled ordinary citizens to gain some of the attributes of a popular tribunate standing up to power while, on the other hand, the movement only gained this foothold because it was not itself popular. #saccageparis’s composition therefore contradicts its tactics, and the movement is best described as “bourgeois populism.” This case shows us how social media’s populist affordances can be exploited by elites and, as a result, offers precious insights for those interested in rescuing social media’s radical-democratic possibilities from elite capture.
items.title: Popular tribunate or bourgeois populism? #saccageparis and social media’s radical-democratic paradox

items.abstract: This interview with the philosopher Raymond Geuss, Professor Emeritus of Philosophy at the University of Cambridge, explores the questions animating his 2026 book Tracks in Chaos: Philosophical Orientation and Political Reflection (Polity). The book's title invokes Heidegger's image of the Holzweg – forest tracks cut through labour that often lead nowhere – which Geuss develops into a figure for philosophy as a historically situated, constrained, and dependent activity rather than an autonomous system. Drawing on his formation in Heidegger, Marx, and Adorno, he defends a suspicion of ordinary language and everyday concepts, proposing a ‘binary vision’ for operating within social practices while seeing through them. He distinguishes three senses of authority, none of which philosophy can claim, and separates ‘moralising’ from moral judgement proper. The interview closes with his diagnosis of a disintegrating West, marked by concentrated wealth and power, financialisation, technological deskilling, and a pervasive loss of orientation.
items.title: Paths to nowhere: An interview with Raymond Geuss about Tracks in Chaos
