items.abstract: This paper argues that both fascist and queer politics are animated by the erotics of transgression: the pleasure that derives from the act of violating normative boundaries concerning gender, sexuality, and the body. Yet while fascism eroticises the restoration of hierarchies of human value, queerness eroticises the destruction of those hierarchical classifications. Against economistic and orthodox psychoanalytic accounts, this paper argues that the erotic charge of transgression emerges from capitalism’s devaluation of embodied needs and desires. By hierarchising needs according to their representability within the terms of value production, capitalism produces a historically specific distinction between profitable and unprofitable needs. Because the body resists full subsumption, many of our bodily needs, desires and capacities are abandoned by capital and can often only be met, if at all, through relations of dependency in the reproductive sphere. It is around this site of abandonment that erotic fantasies of transgression cluster.
items.title: Desire Beyond Value: On Reproduction, Queerness, and (Anti-) Fascism

items.abstract: “Developmentalism” refers to the idea that human societies progress through a series of historical stages, along one path or multiple paths, which allows for the comparison and hierarchization of different populations. As numerous works have shown, developmentalism was often called upon to justify Europe’s domination of non-European populations, which were figured as backward or barbaric. To complicate the commonplace equation of developmentalism and empire, I analyze José Carlos Mariátegui’s political thought as a stratigraphic history in which different temporalities—especially archaic temporality, or the remnants of Incan communalism, and developmental temporality—were vertically stacked and in tension, and I elaborate a conception of what I call “archaic developmentalism.” For Mariátegui, while the past temporality, institutions, and practices of the Incan Empire persisted into the present, he did not perceive them as hurdles to be cleared on the upward march of progress. Rather, as I argue, Mariátegui recognized the political potency of Incan communalism’s remnants—particularly, the ayllu , or Incan communal form—and he conjectured that the collision of temporal-historical lay
items.title: José Carlos Mariátegui’s Archaic Developmentalism: Utopia, the Incan Empire, and Peruvian Reality

items.abstract: Illiberal governments increasingly target universities as sites of political dissent and ideological opposition. This paper compares three illustrative cases—Boğaziçi University under Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Central European University under Viktor Orbán, and elite US universities under Donald Trump—to examine how illiberal governments deploy state power against autonomous, high-profile, liberal-aligned institutions of higher education, and how students and faculty respond. Although universities are not always bastions of pluralism, tolerance, and democracy, attacks on universities are often concurrent with illiberal governance. We argue that illiberal governments perceive universities as vanguards of hegemonic liberalism and as partisan opponents in certain contexts, and that state repression operates along a continuum of coercion, legal displacement, and discursive delegitimation. These attacks on academic autonomy trigger varied responses—from mobilization, to fragmentation, to withdrawal—shaped by domestic political opportunity structures, the intensity of state repression, and campus culture. By conceptualizing the university as a contested political institution rather than a ne
items.title: The War on Universities: Illiberal Tactics in Turkey, Hungary, and the United States

items.abstract: Which kinds of leadership are appropriate for emancipatory politics? Moving beyond a dichotomy of vanguardism and horizontalism, I advance rearguardism. Supplementing vanguardism, rearguardism involves defensive leadership and legitimation of existing movements, protecting these from attacks by dominant forces and actively propagating their struggles without co-opting or directing these from the front. I first outline vanguardism, focusing on the work of Vladimir Lenin and Rosa Luxemburg. I then reconstruct the most prominent account of rearguardism, by Boaventura de Sousa Santos, before arguing that his account is too dematerialised and confined to an epistemic realm. I therefore reformulate a different vision of rearguardism by turning to Antonio Gramsci.
items.title: Rearguard Politics: Rethinking Political Leadership From the Back

items.abstract: Throughout Western democracies, the left remains in political purgatory and without a road towards political power. We examine Chantal Mouffe’s strategy for achieving a left populism with socialist characteristics, followed by Thomas Piketty’s program for ‘participatory socialism’. We highlight the admirable details they offer about alliance politics and transforming property relations. Nevertheless, we argue for why they cannot realise in practice what they hope to achieve, in part because of their respective convictions about the autonomy of the political. Mouffe’s treatment of economic and political liberalism, and her misreading of class relations and neoliberal oligarchy, leave her politics within a liberal capitalist orbit. Piketty’s work is overly idealist and insufficiently critical, and his proposed changes to capitalist and political institutions are too narrow. Their merits notwithstanding, socialist strategy must go beyond Mouffe and Piketty.
items.title: Gaining Power and Using It: the Promise and Limits of Socialism in Mouffe and Piketty

items.abstract: This article argues that UK labour law scholarship has failed to engage sufficiently with Marxian insights about the nature and basis of employer power and exploitation, and about the limits of law as a means through which to overcome them. As a result, it lacks a strategic orientation, commitment to structural change and theoretical foundations that would enable it to overcome the causes of the problems against which labour law is traditionally directed. The article begins by elaborating a Marxian inspired account of employer-power and the associated problem of exploitation, teasing out its strategic implications. It then explores a range of Marxian contributions to the question of the role of law in the struggle for structural change. It then uses insights from this discussion to explain the potentially important role that labour law scholarship might play in advancing such struggles, before exploring whether UK labour law scholarship has ever embraced such a role for itself in practice. Concluding that UK labour law scholarship has never embraced such a role, the article suggests how UK labour law scholarship might more effectively perform such a strategic role today.
items.title: Labour Law, Strategy, and the Structural Critique of Capitalism

items.abstract: In this article, I interrogate the theoretical architecture that underpins three increasingly influential normative prescriptions for a just political configuration in Israel–Palestine: reconciliation, decolonization of relationships, and egalitarian bi-nationalism (RDB-N). Although recent scholarship has attempted to integrate them into a shared framework, they remain insufficiently articulated, delaying the emergence of a transformative praxis. Here, I argue that the core impasse lies in the dominant “top-down” conception of reconciliation, which, by presuming that a postconflict political order is a prerequisite for implementation, produces a dependency that obstructs the normative potential of RDB-N as a coherent framework for structural transformation. In response, I advance a “bottom-up” conception of reconciliation that is both theoretically plausible and normatively desirable. This reimagines reconciliation as an implementation-driven and grassroots dynamic capable of initiating decolonial transformation and prefiguring an egalitarian binational future, rather than a postconflict process led by the state and its institutions. In proposing this theoretical rearticulation, I
items.title: Reconciliation, Decolonization of Relationships, and Egalitarian Bi-nationalism: A Praxis for the Israeli–Palestinian Impasse?

items.abstract: This article offers a feminist reworking of Adriana Cavarero’s conceptualization of horrorism as a form of extreme violence that targets and dehumanizes its victims through dismemberment and an ontological assault on human uniqueness. While Cavarero’s intervention is motivated by a commitment to resisting patriarchal logics of war and reorienting political thought toward care, we argue that her framework depends on an overly fixed opposition between the monstrous perpetrator and the defenseless victim, exemplified in her reading of Medusa in contrast with the Christian Madonna. The binary risks reproducing the very logics of exclusion and moral absolutism it seeks to disrupt. Demonstrating the point, we engage in a critical rereading of Medusa across classical and later interpretive traditions that demonstrates how she cannot be reduced to an emblem of absolute monstrosity, but instead appears as a plural figure: victim, goddess, protector, and generative presence—as well as a destructive monster. This reading destabilizes Cavarero’s conceptualization of both horrorism and victimhood, revealing the political and narrative instability of these categories. In reaction, we develop a f
items.title: Care and Contemporary Violence: Deconstructing the Monstrous in/as Cavarero’s Horrorism

items.abstract: The epistocracy debate has turned largely on the character of the electorate—what voters know, whether competence filters can be designed well, and what filtered selection produces. Another strand has focused on the legitimacy of epistocratic justifications. I ask instead about the equilibrium effects of the institution. Epistocracy shifts some political authority from the median voter toward citizens selected on competence grounds, and existing critiques press legitimational, epistemic, abuse‐based, and demographic objections against such proposals. I develop a different objection, focusing on one especially plausible form of epistocracy: Jason Brennan's epistocratic veto , a competence‐selected council empowered to override legislation it judges incompetent. Drawing on Acemoglu and Robinson's account of democratization, I argue that the franchise solves a credible‐commitment problem between elites and the poor under conditions of revolutionary threat: universal suffrage puts redistributive authority in majority hands in a way elites cannot easily reverse, because reversing it requires revoking the franchise itself. The institutionally realistic veto hands some of that authority b
items.title: Epistocracy and the Commitment Problem

items.abstract: The work of being an elected representative today is increasingly demanding as they seek to perform representation amid political distrust, polarised electorates, and rising populism. In response, elected representatives and their teams invest heavily in developing and showcasing their capacities to represent. This variously involves constructing representative personas, designing participatory events, curating diverse digital content, and communicating evidence on how and where they are representing. Extending Saward’s representative claim-making framework, this article develops the concept of representative-capacity-making to better understand this overlooked (‘backstage’) aspect of modern representation. The article explores – in concept only – the work involved in developing and demonstrating four key representative capacities. The normative implications of representative-capacity-making in an era of democratic strain are considered. While representative-capacity-making can be read as a response to the challenges of democratic representation today, the extent to which it can be a solution is mixed, in specified ways.
items.title: Representative-capacity-making: The strategic backstage work of political representation

items.abstract: This article examines the significance of maritime imaginaries in the work and life of Walter Benjamin, arguing that the various references to the sea and ships across his writings serve as more than mere metaphorical content. Drawing on Benjamin’s personal experiences of sea travel, the article contends that his conceptual framework, particularly his historical method of rescue ( Rettung ), is intimately tied to the materiality and embodied experience of mobility at sea. The analysis contrasts Benjamin’s position – as one clinging to the mast of a shipwreck – with the classical philosophical tradition of detached spectatorship, asserting that he mobilizes the unstable maritime space as a theatre of crisis and a source of alternative knowledge. It explores how Benjamin saw maritime oral cultures and the sailor’s perspective as providing an essential counter-discourse to bourgeois notions of travel and a key to understanding the decline of storytelling ( Erzählung ) in the modern age.
items.title: Walter Benjamin’s Maritime Imaginaries

items.abstract: In the Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals , Kant names beneficence, or promotion of another’s happiness, as the way we attain “positive” agreement with the humanity in another person (GMS 4:430). I argue, however, that beneficence is not the only way, or necessarily the preferred way, to secure this. By exploring the discussions of commerce and interaction found in Kant’s later practical philosophy, particularly the section on cosmopolitan right in the Metaphysics of Morals , I show that Kant makes available a substantively different way we can positively express recognition of others as ends in themselves. This alternative emphasizes not promoting another’s happiness but instead letting others influence both one’s own ends and other aspects of one’s identity.
items.title: Beyond Beneficence: Commerce and Interaction in Relation to Kant’s Formula of Humanity

items.abstract: Drawing from Kant’s philosophy of history, this article defends the view that, if peace is a duty, war cannot be a right. I argue that (1) (perpetual) peace can be accounted for as a historical duty : a goal that humankind ought to achieve throughout a historically situated process of moralization – according to the moral vocation of the human being itself – that essentially relies on juridical and political conditions. I then argue that (2) war represents a collective state of minority based on the inversion of the maxims of enlightened reason, of common human understanding, of wisdom. The upshot is that (3) war is always a practice contrary to morals and the seal of the breakdown of practical rationality and all bonds of community. Following Kant, the only viable option is international law in a cosmopolitical framework, whereby the rule of law ought to take war’s place as the means to the solution of all controversies.
items.title: The Duty of Peace and the Minority of War. Arguments From Kant

items.abstract: Maurizio Ferraris’ “new realism” rejects postmodern constructionism and insists on the unamendable independence of reality. Yet his dismissal of interpretation-friendly ontological accounts as inherently anti-realist overlooks richer possibilities within the hermeneutic tradition. I argue that Luigi Pareyson’s hermeneutic ontology provides the missing ground for Ferraris’ strong realist insights. Through a triadic analysis in which I pair Ferraris’ concepts of unamendability , positivity , and documentality with Pareyson’s treatment of inexhaustibility , congeniality , and testimoniality , respectively, I demonstrate that to interpret is to participate in the active constitution and disclosure of the real. Pareyson’s theory of “ontological personalism” effectively shows that the resistance of reality derives from its relational excess, not abstract independence. Synthesizing their views yields a realist hermeneutics capable of affirming truth’s binding character while recognizing the situated and plural nature of all knowledge claims. Against naïve objectivism and subjective relativism alike, Pareyson carves a fruitful path for contemporary debates about the nature of reality, scie
items.title: Realist Hermeneutics: Pareyson’s Challenge to New Realism

items.abstract: This paper presents a pragmatist interpretation of John Stuart Mill’s arguments defending freedom of expression, drawing a comparison between Mill’s arguments in On Liberty and the work of Charles Peirce. I argue that Mill’s commitment to fallibilism in his argument for supporting free expression is more closely aligned with pragmatist concerns for collaborative inquiry than the liberal concern of mediating competing perspectives. This interpretation is supported by key contingencies in Mill’s argument, framed by his assumption that freedom of opinion facilitates a pursuit of truth. Exposure of such contingencies provides the basis for a more precise theoretical groundwork for outlining limits of free speech without necessary reference to Mill’s harm principle, with freedom of opinion being contingent upon said opinion’s pragmatic contribution to collaborative inquiry in the collective pursuit of truth. Freedom of opinion entails being receptive to genuine doubt and remaining open to revising our personal commitments and opinions.
items.title: Mill’s Pragmatism on Free Speech and Inquiry

items.abstract: With its Afrological roots, debates about jazz improvisation almost invariably involve a discussion of freedom. This article argues that jazz improvisation is not concerned with individual liberty but focused on collective escape. This article proposes that improvisation is politically efficacious insofar that it is the motor of perennial revolution. That improvisation can transform apparatus of control from within is optimistic. Connecting Gilles Deleuze’s conception of exhaustion with Fred Moten's notion of escape, however, tempers this optimism and describes the ardour of the task. The variation of musical structures – and the habituated social relations to which they are tied – is exhausted by improvisation. This is not a destructive process but a creative one, producing novel connections and spaces in which political communities can be reimagined. Improvisation does not install some new hierarchy but opens itself to this same exhaustive process.
items.title: Exhaustion and Escape: The Political Efficacy of Jazz Improvisation

items.abstract: This article argues that Carl Schmitt’s approach to the visual expression of political power evolves from an early reliance on symbolic form to a later adoption of allegory, influenced by Walter Benjamin. Initially attracted to the Catholic Church as a symbolic synthesis of bureaucracy and charisma, Schmitt grew disillusioned with its modes of visual representation. He then turned to political myth, envisioning the national leader as the symbolic incarnation of a unified people. This model, however, also proved untenable. In search of an alternative, Schmitt drew on Benjamin’s theory of allegory to retrieve the Baroque tradition of state personification: Sovereigns, like actors on a stage, outwardly represent the state without claiming to exhaust its meaning. I contend that this allegorical framework allowed Schmitt not only to sidestep the totalizing tendencies of political myth but also to open a conceptual path for reimagining Europe’s postwar fractured space.
items.title: The Visibility of the State: Symbolic and Allegorical Representations in the Work of Carl Schmitt

items.abstract: As a well-known neo-Marxist critical theorist from Eastern Europe, Zygmunt Bauman continues reflecting on aesthetic issues. On the basis of sociology of knowledge, especially Antonio Gramsci's theory of intellectuals, he establishes the intimate relation between this knowledge and aesthetic autonomy and develops the understanding of aesthetic modernity. He deeply explores the transformation from the aesthetic legislators in modernity to interpreters in postmodernity. It is obvious that there is some continuity in his whole theory from the 1960s to the new century. The continuity is evident from the perspective of sociology of knowledge, especially of aesthetic knowledge. With the critical sociology of knowledge, semantic analysis and cultural anthropology, Bauman provides a new paradigm for contemporary aesthetics and a new version of critical theory in his over sixty of years academic life.
items.title: Zygmunt Bauman's sociology of aesthetic knowledge

items.abstract: This paper offers a critical reflection on Zygmunt Bauman's diagnosis of digital modernity, particularly his concern with the erosion of privacy in an era of confessional culture and performative self-disclosure. Engaging Bauman's work alongside thinkers such as Blumenberg, Honneth, Arendt and Thompson, it explores visibility as an anthropological and political condition. The paper fields the notion of ‘prepositional sociology’, inspired by Maria Markus, as a mode of analysis that foregrounds the creative capacities of individuals to construct meaningful lives despite the pressures of a commodified, surveillant world. In this context, friendship is discussed as a form of non-instrumental intimacy that resists the logic of economic rationality. The paper seeks to contribute to a critical sociology that recognises both the dehumanising dynamics of modernity and the ordinary practices that exceed them.
items.title: Reflections on Zygmunt Bauman: Visibility, privacy and prepositional sociology

items.abstract: This article contests the tendency to see Islam as overwhelmingly collective and theorizes the individual from Islamic history and tradition of thought. It does so by recovering and recasting the ideas of Abul Hashim (1905–1974), a prominent South Asian anticolonial Muslim thinker and political actor. It examines how Hashim reconstructs Qur’anic ideas to oppose modern individualism primarily due to its loss of moral unity and advances a theory of the individual that argues for a unified ethical framework, which binds the individual, God, and others in an embedded relationship of love and care in the community. The article explores a unique trajectory for self-constitution developed within Islamic history and tradition—a trajectory that goes beyond the rise of the autonomous, reflexive, and self-serving individual without compromising the importance of one’s intention and conscience in shaping the self. This theory of the individual from the Islamic tradition refutes the Eurocentric framework of theorizing the concept by presenting a distinct framework that transcends the dichotomy between the individual and the community, a battle that is pervasive in contemporary Euro-American pol
items.title: Theorizing the Individual in Anticolonial Muslim Thought

items.abstract: During the first decades of the twentieth century, the word “democracy” was rarely used to describe existing political systems. Rather, it was usually employed polemically to criticize European parliamentary regimes for their incapacity to actualize the principle of popular power. Critiques of parliamentarism in the name of democracy were numerous and came from all sides of the political spectrum. This paper analyses them through the lens offered by debates about the use of the referendum. The “direct appeal to the people” was widely discussed at the turn between the nineteenth and twentieth centuries: It was the lowest common denominator of otherwise highly divergent political projects, all of which appealed to democracy to overcome the failures of parliamentarism. Yet their diagnoses of what was wrong with parliamentary regimes differed widely, as did their interpretations of the democratic nature of the referendum. In what follows, I will analyze three different critiques of parliamentarism, and their corresponding theories of democracy, as outlined through debates about the referendum in Europe from 1890 to 1935.
items.title: “Barricades Across the Road to Democracy”: The Referendum and the Crisis of Parliamentarism in Europe, 1890–1930

items.abstract: How to address the grief that attends the inevitable loss in war of those we love? How to turn victims of war into heroes? How to resolve the agonizing choices that war imposes on us? Euripides’s Iphigenia at Aulis , the tale of Agamemnon’s sacrifice of his daughter, and Pericles’s Funeral Oration as imagined by Thucydides were both written during the Peloponnesian War, and each points to the creation of stories told to assuage the grief that follows the loss of loved ones and to obscure the challenging moral choices that wars demand. Euripides’s characters are trapped by the moral ambiguities that plague our political decision-making and, through a startling conclusion to the play that recalls the language of Pericles’s Funeral Oration, they welcome the “vain myths” we introduce to make our wartime decisions seem painless and our moral dilemmas disappear. Only the mother Clytemnestra refuses to be lulled by the stories or disappear happily within the walls of her palace. The tragedian can give full voice to the complex role of those stories; the rhetoric of the political leader obscures the ambiguity and “vanity” of those myths. Given the wide familiarity with Pericles’s Funeral O
items.title: The Stories We Tell: Euripides’s Iphigenia at Aulis and Pericles’s Funeral Oration

items.abstract: This article returns to Zygmunt Bauman's lifelong search for politics through the lens of disability, arguing that disability is not marginal to his social theory but revelatory to its moral core. Bauman's essay ‘Society Enables and Disables’ is read alongside major contributions from Disability Studies to reconstruct the philosophical anthropology that underpins Bauman's liquid period: a humanism not grounded in labour or productivity, but in mutual enablement and interdependence. Disability exposes the mutual economy of worth that structured life across solid and liquid modernity alike, illustrating how productivism continues to invalidate us. It builds upon Beilharz's claim that socialism is a principle rather than a programme, it argues that a politics adequate to liquid modernity must be anti-productivist. In the context of automation and artificial intelligence, it proposes a liquid socialism grounded in interdependence committed to opening the social question beyond labour.
items.title: Still in search of politics: Disability, productivism, and socialism in liquid modernity

items.abstract: While abolition and revolution might appear complementary, it is not always easy to see how they can relate with each other as part of a coherent conception of emancipatory struggle, nor how such complementarity might inform political strategy. In response to this problem, the objective of this paper is to contribute to a critical reappraisal of the revolutionary heritage of abolitionist thought by drawing attention to what Joy James called ‘the revolutionary era’ of abolitionist politics of the late 1960s and early 1970s USA, focusing on the organisational politics of George Jackson who I consider to be one of the period’s most original thinkers. The claim I would like the reader to consider is that the type of vanguardism once presented by revolutionary abolitionists like George Jackson can help us to re-evaluate the political and ideological basis upon which a greater socialisation of struggles can be built today in view of the constitution of potential counter-hegemonic blocks capable of contesting the demands that capital makes on the planet and our lives. To put it in broader terms, the paper hopes to contribute to a widening of the conversation on how the question of aboliti
items.title: ‘Seize the Time’ – Abolition & Revolution at the Crossroads

items.abstract: In recent years, states have expanded their formal legal powers to strip their subjects of citizenship. But should states have the power to revoke citizenship? If so, how may this power be permissibly exercised, and how ought it to be constrained? This article argues that some standard critiques of denationalization face some important limitations. These limitations stem from the fact that these critiques fail to identify the distinctiveness of citizenship as a status, and, thus, fail to identify an objection that is directly connected with citizenship loss. To supplement these critiques, I offer a framework for understanding the value of citizenship, which draws attention to the egalitarian functions of citizenship. This yields a novel interpretation and defense of the charge that denationalization is problematically inegalitarian: viz., denationalization threatens to impair the egalitarian functions of citizenship.
items.title: What is wrong with denationalization: Citizenship revocation and social equality

items.abstract: Recently, political theorists have been increasingly concerned with the implications of democratic values for work. This article contributes to these debates by examining the main vehicle through which workers, historically, have sought democracy at work: the labor union. The article defends a vision of economic democracy that arises from the practice of labor unions. It then emphasizes the distinctive features of labor unions that make them potential vehicles for democracy in other domains. Labor unions are particularly important means of advancing democratic values for three reasons: (1) their ability to appeal to the short- and mid-term self-interest of their members; (2) their anchor in the material reproduction of society; and (3) that they rely on attitudes of cooperation and solidarity among their members. Yet these three features also point to potential limitations of labor unions as laboratories of democracy.
items.title: A Democratic Theory of Labor Unions

items.abstract: Stasis amidst crisis defines the present conjuncture, while the left seems trapped in a fractured sequence between short-lived and fundamentally constrained uprisings and electoral bids. This essay attempts to define the terrain of contemporary struggles in reference to their impasses, especially as these relate to transformations in capitalist nation-states. Tracing the limits of opposed strategic poles – a strong ‘protective’ state and ‘prolonged’ forms of dual power – it situates their common turn to social reproduction struggles and criticises their common presupposition: that states have abandoned core aspects of social reproduction, opening new paths for resistance. Instead we have ‘organised abandonment’: the developing, if still contradictory, integration of state capacities and international capital, extending into new modalities of social reproduction. State capacities have come to be structured in ways that impose impasses on traditional aims of working-class autonomy. In this light, the key strategic question is how we can conceive of an ascending sequence of struggles.
items.title: Strategy at an Impasse: Prolonged Dual Power, State Capacities and Social Reproduction Struggles

items.abstract: This paper analyzes the repression of Palestine solidarity activism on UK university campuses following October 7, 2023. To explain why institutions whose mission centers on critical inquiry and open debate have enacted far-reaching restrictions on Palestine solidarity, we compile an original dataset of 114 incidents across 70 universities (October 2023–March 2025). Drawing on Jacques Rancière’s concept of the “distribution of the sensible,” we conceptualize repression not simply as deterrence or punishment but as a mode of aesthetic ordering through which universities govern political visibility and legitimacy. Repression is multilayered, operating through coercive enforcement and legal actions, procedural and bureaucratic controls, punitive disciplinary processes, and the symbolic erasure of visual and affective expressions of dissent. These practices are enabled by—and in turn reinforce—neoliberal managerialism, racialized securitization, and imperial governance logics that produce racialized hierarchies of threat and safety and recode solidarity as risk and disruption. By rendering Palestine solidarity illegible and illegitimate as politics, UK universities contribute to condit
items.title: Repression as Aesthetic Ordering: How UK Universities Make Palestine Solidarity Illegible in a Time of Genocide

items.abstract: This article discusses the concept of strategy and how contemporary military thinking can contribute to strategy from below. First it discusses the military lineages of the term ‘strategy’. Second, the evolution of its meaning and its entry into the labour movement. Third, the relationship with ‘tactics’. Fourth, it analyses the concept of ‘operational art’ and explores how it can be used outside the military field. Fifth, it reviews some key debates on contemporary military strategy to enrich the understanding of strategy. Sixth, it explores new military analogies based on the concepts of asymmetric, unrestricted and hybrid warfare. Finally, it considers the term ‘grand strategy’ to assess its value for strategy from below.
items.title: On Strategy: Thinking with the Military

items.abstract: This article examines dystopian literature as a critical counterpart to sociology, emphasizing its role in social self-description. The author introduces the concept of the sublimation of the negative, inspired by Niklas Luhmann, to explain how dystopias transform the negative side of self-descriptive social codes into tools for critical thought. The re-introduction of the distinction of good/evil allows dystopia to unmask the latent ‘social evil’ hidden within the utopias of efficiency promoted by other systems such as politics, science, or the economy, which are often blind to their own human costs. Unlike sociology, which often avoids speculative and future-oriented inquiries, dystopias embrace imaginative alternatives, addressing epistemic gaps such as de-futurization and the marginalization of subjective experience. Through analyses of works such as Gabriel de Tarde's The Underground Man , Edward Morgan Forster's The Machine Stops and Janusz A. Zajdel's Limes inferior , the article demonstrates dystopia's ability to transcend sociological explanatory schemes.
items.title: Dystopia and the limits of sociological thought: A critical exploration

items.abstract: This article is about a critique of capitalism I call the politics of racial despair, which sought to resurrect a racially defined culture against the impersonal domination of capital. This argument helps us understand an underlying logic behind racist critiques of markets, and I show how the politics of racial despair appealed to white racial identity to reenchant capitalism's decontextualized social relations. I discuss an example of the politics of racial despair forged in the Depression-era American South: the political theory of Donald Davidson, a member of the Southern Agrarians. Drawing on archival material, I show how the Southern Agrarians were part of a transnational politics of racial despair that sought to counter impersonal domination with a return to allegedly concrete forms of life—subsistence production and mythologies of race. Today, we see the stirrings of this racialized critique of capitalism. Davidson's political thought serves as a reminder that not all critiques of capitalism stem from a concern with equality or freedom, but can also serve malign ends.
items.title: Racial anticapitalism during the Great Depression

items.abstract: This paper explores the idea that technical progress could free humanity from necessity and labour. Taking inspiration from a remark in Arendt's Human Condition , I consider a tension immanent to that idea: the possibility that its realisation requires social transformations that culminate in a world incommensurable with our own and to which our concepts of freedom no longer apply. Drawing on resources from social theory, the philosophy of technology and critical theory, I defend this incommensurability thesis in two steps. I argue, first, that technical progress entails a social dynamic which leads to continuous upward shifts in the level of automation required to free people from work, plausibly extending beyond the sphere of production; second, that this leads the idea of freedom from labour ad absurdum : the widespread automation of human life would render modern concepts of freedom unintelligible.
items.title: Can technical progress make us free? On the idea of freedom from labour

items.abstract: Over the last few decades, interconnected debates about Scottish independence and Brexit have shaped politics in the United Kingdom and raised questions of constituent power that remain controversial both politically and theoretically. Against this backdrop, this article proposes a nuanced democratic conception of constituent power that serves as an alternative to orthodox sovereigntist accounts. This conception is theoretically more compelling and, moreover, enables fruitful engagement with contemporary constitutional controversies. By establishing a dialogue between theoretical discussion and the Scottish and UK case, the article, first, explores constituent power as one dimension of popular sovereignty and its interplay with constituted powers over time. Second, it examines how constituent collectives can and, in recent history, have become subject to contestation and change. Third, it sketches monist and pluralist conceptions of constituent power and peoples that co-exist, yet conflict within the United Kingdom, thereby mapping distinct trajectories for possible constitutional futures in a union setting.
items.title: Constituent power and constituent collectives in a Union context: Deciding the futures of Scotland and the United Kingdom

items.abstract: Is the strategic question back on the agenda? Construed as awareness of the relative autonomy of political intervention, its return presents a challenge. Amid persistent but fragile neo-liberal hegemony, vigorous but scattered social struggles, and alternatives that are theoretically developed but disconnected from real conditions, strategy involves reinventing the ways and means of an effective break with the capitalist organisation of the world. Reconsidering the classical question of property in conjunction with the production and reproduction of labour-power, I shall endeavour to show that the perspective of reappropriation can unify existing mobilisations without infringing their autonomy or forsaking their aggressive political structuration. To this end, I shall suggest a critical analysis of the theses of Negri and Hardt on the common, in as much as they invite us to re-read Marx from the political and strategic angle of social reappropriation as both means and end of collective and individual emancipation.
items.title: Towards a Communist Strategy of Reappropriation

items.abstract: The current hegemonic crisis of neoliberal capitalism has relaunched debates on socialist strategy. These discussions have largely crystallised around a polarisation between a ‘democratic road’ to socialism and the insurrectionary approach associated with Lenin and Trotsky. This article seeks to problematise that polarisation and to advance an alternative perspective. It does so by rethinking the concept of dual power not as the embryonic form of a new state nor as entirely external to existing institutions, but as a centralised organ of power from below, capable of autonomous initiative, through which mass radicalisation can most fully express itself in moments of intensified class struggle.
items.title: Antinomies of Socialist Strategy?

items.abstract: Prefigurative politics, the belief in and commitment to an identity or accord between present political action and a desired future (or between means and ends), has become a significant preoccupation of social movement theory and practice. Understood as demanding the deliberate implementation of future social relations in the present, it often appears as an explicit criticism of Marxism, even of strategic politics in general. For this reason it has often been rejected by Marxists as idealist, utopian or voluntarist. Against this framing, this article makes the case that there are resources within the tradition of revolutionary Marxism for thinking about prefigurative politics. These in turn can help us reflect on strategic debates within and across the radical left. The article traces the outlines of a Marxist approach to prefigurative politics, rooted in concepts of revolutionary practice and self-emancipation as collective learning processes. Finally, it considers how these ideas can inform broader strategic debates.
items.title: On ‘The Real Movement Which Abolishes the Present State of Things’: Marxism and Prefigurative Politics

items.abstract: While the 2024 Gaza solidarity encampments and campus occupations before them have been the objects of significant debate among academics and broader public audiences, the spatialized and radical democratic dimensions of these protests remain undertheorized. This article argues that turning to Henri Lefebvre provides valuable tools for better understanding campus occupations and answering the questions that universities face today. Grounded in Lefebvre’s comments about students, knowledge production, and campus life following May 1968, I argue that the university is a key site for demanding, clarifying, and expanding the “right to the city.” Extending Lefebvre’s analysis through a discussion of the spatial production activities of contemporary elite North American universities, I propose a novel “right to the campus” defined by radical democratization of university governance and use-driven spatial design. Finally, I draw lessons from the 1968 Columbia University occupations before applying the right to the campus to analyze the successes and disappointments of the more recent wave of encampments. items.abstract: Big data and empirical social science share an often-subterraneous assumption, namely, positivism. Some of their jointly hidden premises are that experiences, preferences, and culture are all equally quantifiable, testable, and measurable. Further, their view is a reification of the status quo, a harmonistic view of society. On the other hand, the critical view espouses social antagonism , the view that society essentially consists of a struggle between groups. Critical theory argues against the critical rationalists that positivism (and thus, empirical social science) is guilty of a political agnosticism and, therefore, services the ends of bureaucracy and administration. This paper draws out some latent beliefs of big data as a new version of positivism and shows that big data inherits the problems of empirical social science. In particular, algorithms and data analytics for predictive policing, aggressively personalized advertisement, and prison recidivism stand out as substantial evidence of the new positivism that surges in administered society.
items.title: The New Positivism: A Hegelian Critique

items.abstract: This article examines the semantic structure of the left-right political binary in contemporary Anglophone discourse. It argues that the fusion of “right” as directional orientation with “right” as moral correctness produces a form of semantic over-determination that complicates the articulation of democratic legitimacy in periods of political crisis. The claim is not that directional metaphors determine political outcomes, but that they furnish a discursive resource that can be mobilized in struggles over authority, order, and rectitude. To illuminate the contingency of this fusion, the article turns to the East Asian concept of zheng 正 (uprightness), whose semantic independence from handedness reveals that the association between direction and correctness is historically specific rather than conceptually necessary. Rather than proposing zheng as a replacement for the left-right political vocabulary, the article develops it as a diagnostic lens through which to distinguish questions of moral correctness, political legitimacy, and political orientation that English tends to conflate. By placing the Confucian doctrine of zhengming (Rectification of Names) into dialogue with contempo
items.title: Upright: Zheng 正 and the Semantics of Political Legitimacy

items.abstract: This paper contributes to contemporary debates in political theory about the power of business corporations by offering a genealogy of the corporation through the lens of a series of historical mutations of the corporate form. Originally, there were two corporate forms, both non-profit: member corporations (today's associations) and property corporations (today's charitable foundations). The contemporary business corporation arguably is a hybrid of both of these original forms, introducing unique commercial features (shares with profit distribution rights that are transferable). These commercial features are largely responsible for the corporation's extractive nature, that is, its tendency to prey on non-shareholder interests. The future of the corporation may well lie in a partial return to the two original non-profit forms. Two corporate forms developed in the nineteenth century can provide the format for such a return: cooperatives (which reinforce the idea of membership) and foundation-owned companies. items.title: The corporation—a return to origins?

items.abstract: Previous scholarship on Caesarism has focused overwhelmingly on continental Europe. Insofar as Britain has been mentioned at all, it has been as a mere foil to the latter: ostensibly, the kind of democratic dictatorship known as “Caesarism” was wholly alien to British traditions of limited, representative, and parliamentary government; as such, the British dismissed it out of hand; the concept never gained any purchase within British thought; indeed, the word itself was not even used in Britain until 1857 (according to the OED , cited by several scholars). By drawing on an array of periodical and newspaper sources, the proposed contribution will challenge this orthodoxy along three principal lines: first, it will demonstrate that Auguste Romieu’s L’ère des Césars (1850) was widely reviewed in Britain, with the result that both the word and the concept of “Caesarism” passed immediately into British usage; second, it will demonstrate that rather than merely dismissing the concept out of hand, mid-century British thinkers engaged seriously with it, formulating an elaborate critique of “Caesarism” as practiced on the Continent; third, it will demonstrate that, as the century wore on, a

items.abstract: We use economic experiments to study a fundamental question in political economy: Do voters understand the benefits of taxes? Participants play an economic game as members of a virtual society composed of computer players. In each round, the players earn low or high income, see the distribution of income, and then vote for low or high taxes. We test whether participants vote rationally for high taxes when poor and low taxes when rich, following a classic model in political economy, or whether they focus on the burden of taxes more than the benefits. Across three experiments, poor players voted against high taxes 30% to 50% of the time, and they were more opposed when the same policy was labeled “taxes” than when it was labeled “sharing.” In Experiment 2, Singaporean participants opposed taxes at about the same rate as those of Americans in Experiment 1. In Experiment 3, participants’ opposition to taxes persisted when they received low income every round. These results support the burden hypothesis: voters focus more on the burden of paying taxes than on the benefits they provide. We reflect on what the results imply for the politics of taxes.
items.title: Do Voters Understand the Benefits of Taxes?

items.abstract: The defense of gay rights and other liberal values by some right-wing populists is often perceived as an opportunistic strategy to justify anti-Muslim policies. But this explanation for co-optation of liberal values by parties that are considered to be in conflict with liberalism circumvents a proper analysis of the phenomenon. I will therefore investigate this element within populist politics as a problem of liberalism, rather than of populism. Doing so, this paper holds that co-optation of liberal values by right-wing populists follows from a distinctly liberal dialectic and, genealogically, represents a distinct strand of liberalism. Firstly, I will discuss the origins of populism in the Netherlands and present them as an exemplary case of what Adam Tebble calls “identity liberalism.” Secondly, I will analyze two foundational texts of the Dutch Party for Freedom to demonstrate its indebtedness to liberalism, and the correspondence of its argumentation to the philosophical problem known as the Böckenförde dilemma. Finally, I will show how identity liberalism is a conceivable, although not necessary, response to this dilemma. The politicization of liberal values by right-wing popu

items.abstract: Many authoritarian regimes originating in violent rebellion are exceptionally durable. Yet others collapse quickly after their birth. We argue that the structure of the founding rebellion explains these divergent trajectories by shaping power-sharing dynamics in the new regime and the nature of conflict recurrence. Regimes founded by unified rebellions (single armed group) usually become highly durable autocracies because their members can credibly share power within the same armed organization. By contrast, regimes founded by fractured rebellions (multiple armed groups) often fail quickly because armed rivals must attempt to share power across their organizations, prompting defections and recurrent rebellions. Empirically, we support these arguments by analyzing originally compiled data on every regime founded by successful rebellion worldwide from 1900 to 2020. Neither alternative rebellion characteristics, like social revolution or leftist ideology, nor country-level factors can explain why rebel regimes follow divergent trajectories.
items.title: Rebel Victory and Authoritarian (Dis)Order

items.abstract: This paper introduces “nihilistic authoritarianism” as a useful concept for political analysis. This term has not been employed before in the scholarly literature, even though the basic idea is familiar from the history of political thought. It is not unusual to say that authoritarians desire power for its own sake. But the basic nihilism of such an idea has not been adequately analyzed. This idea is distinguished from “Platonic authoritarianism,” which consolidates power around a teleological commitment to a set of ethical values or social goals that transcends the political realm. Nihilistic authoritarianism is different. It is “autotelic” in the sense that it does not seek to actualize some further telos or to satisfy some principled justificatory schema. It also tends to consider political power as “autonomous” in the sense that “the political” is severed from other systems of value. Because of its strangeness, nihilistic authoritarianism is often misunderstood and misdiagnosed. items.title: Nihilistic Authoritarianism: Power as an End-in-Itself

items.abstract: This article comprises an interview with Brenna Bhandar, Wendy Brown, and Robert Nichols by Andreas Folkers and Alain Pottage. It seeks to identify the conjuncture that has prompted the contemporary resurgence of questions of property in social theory. It takes critical work on the ‘colonial lives of property’ (Bhandar), neoliberalism (Brown), and colonial dispossession (Nichols) as a vantage point from which to identify the potentials and challenges of an ecological critique of property. The current planetary formation of property cannot be understood without taking into account the ways capitalism and colonialism have insinuated themselves into the material fabric of the Earth.

items.abstract: The average citizen scores poorly on tests that measure political knowledge. Does this suggest anything about whether such citizens are politically competent? In this paper, I argue that citizens are so competent, despite lacking what is typically construed as “political knowledge.” This is because citizens possess a kind of knowledge in common, one that has yet to be taken seriously by skeptics and supporters of democracy alike: citizens have knowledge of other persons, which grounds their politically-salient competence for mutual consideration.

items.abstract: This article reflects on my intellectual journey into cultural sociology and the work of Jeffrey C. Alexander. Beginning with an ethnographic study of theatre for young audiences, I describe how encounters with the Strong Program in Cultural Sociology opened new analytical possibilities for understanding how meaning emerges in the stage−audience encounter. From this point, the value of an ethnographic perspective on civil sphere theory, which I call civil sphere ethnography, helps to bring the civil sphere into view within everyday situations, interactions and emotional dynamics. The article provides an example of how processes of civil repair can occur in a local educational setting within contemporary Swedish society, characterized by increasing diversity and segregation. By connecting Alexander with Paulo Freire, I outline a pedagogical approach I call the critical pedagogy of multicultural incorporation, highlighting its potential to foster recognition, reduce shame, enhance a sense of belonging and, hopefully, broaden civil inclusion.

Habermas’ move from communicative action to inquiring into the pre-political foundations of democracy takes Western philosophy to task but does not push the envelope far enough. Sections from The Philosophical Discourse of Modernity and an interview with Eduardo Mendieta (titled A Conversation About God and the World ) reveal an extant Eurocentric bias. I show that these very same texts contain strands that redeem critical theory for the contemporary, multicultural world(s) we inhabit today. I then take up Dr. B. R. Ambedkar—an Indian pragmatist contemporaneous with the Frankfurt School—as an example of how critical theory (by Max Horkheimer’s principles) might be done in a different cultural setting while remaining pragmatically sensitive to its particularities.

items.abstract: This essay argues that hunger functions as one of the primary passions driving political association in Thomas Hobbes’s materialist political philosophy. Despite the extensive scholarly focus on fear and the social contract, the pivotal role of bodily needs—particularly hunger—in shaping Hobbes’s entire political framework remains underexamined. By attending closely to hunger within Hobbes’s political thought, we can understand how his metaphysical materialism directly informed his political ideas, providing unique insights into the bodily basis of political legitimacy and prefiguring later materialist philosophies. The analysis critically engages with Samantha Frost’s materialist interpretation of Hobbes whilst also incorporating insights from Gregory Kavka and contemporary phenomenological approaches to embodied vulnerability. Through an examination of seventeenth-century English economic conditions, and drawing on Maurice Merleau-Ponty’s phenomenological work, the essay demonstrates that, according to Hobbes, political legitimacy fundamentally depends on the sovereign’s ability to ensure not just survival, but also the material conditions that enable a “delightful living.” This

items.abstract: This article starts from the continuing pertinence of Daniel Bensaïd’s notion of the ‘strategic hypothesis’. To the hypotheses suggested by Bensaïd, it adds another hypothesis, that of ‘left government’, retracing the complex and uneven relation between Marxism and questions of governance. It revisits the ways strategic questions have been posed since the early 2000s, stressing that the strategic debate in the Marxist Left never really took off. As a result, the question of left government was posed in the mid-20omg10s in a terrain marked by a deficient strategic debate, leading to a series of failures and defeats. The article then attempts to point to some crucial strategic lines of demarcation for the reopening of the strategic debate.
items.title: Revolutionary Strategy Revisited: Strategic Hypotheses and Open Questions

items.abstract: The European Commission has argued that the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) adopted in 2018 created a solid framework of digital trust. This paper critically examines the statement. Firstly, a Kantian approach to trust is outlined. In the second section, key aspects of the historical development of commercial trade in personal data and the regulatory efforts of the EU are analyzed. The third part of the paper considers the concept of consent both as a philosophical concept and as the main legal tool for protecting citizens’ data, arguing that the idea that citizens are able to make rational and informed choices about consent to sharing of data is currently fictitious. The final section draws on the Kantian conception of trust to evaluate the EU’s efforts to enable trustworthy data stewardship for its citizens in the digital information environment. The Kantian analysis concludes that even though the GDPR has the potential to supply citizens with trustworthy data protection, its enforcement procedures as well as the 2025 proposed amendments to the GDPR work against trustworthy data stewardship.
items.title: The EU Model of Digital Trust: A Kantian View on EU’s Recommendation of Citizens’ Trust in the GDPR

items.abstract: Contrary to the notion of collective self-rule, in modern democratic states the set of individuals that make the rules and the set of individuals to whom rules apply cannot be one and the same. Recognizing this “non-identity thesis” has important implications for democratic theory. Among them is the need to recognize that any democratic system will involve rule over others and that democratic procedures will not be sufficient for political legitimacy.
items.title: Democracy and Rule over Others: The Boundary Problem and the Limits of Collective Self-Rule

items.abstract: This article challenges the view that Adorno and Deleuze represent antithetical positions, arguing that both share the goal of harnessing the unconscious as a resource for critique. To reconstruct and relate their accounts, it looks beyond Freud to their readings of Kant. It shows that both thinkers appropriate psychoanalysis to actualize latent potentials within the “Copernican turn,” thereby rethinking critique. Adorno locates this potential in reason, transforming the thing-in-itself into a thinking of nonidentity. To this end, he politicizes Freud’s theory of symptom interpretation by reading suffering as an index of social pathologies. Deleuze, by contrast, focuses on sensibility, reworking Freud’s theory of the death drive to radicalize Kantian aesthetics into a productive thinking that unfolds desire. The article concludes by historicizing these accounts—Adorno in relation to fascism and the culture industry, Deleuze in relation to May ’68—and evaluates the contemporary significance of the unconscious for social criticism.
items.title: The Unconscious of Critique: Adorno and Deleuze as Readers of Kant and Freud

items.abstract: This text proposes an understanding of hegemony not as a concept, theory or historical narrative, but as a distinctive method of political work. It thematises this strategic perspective in terms of four central dimensions of Gramsci’s political thought in the Prison Notebooks : the goal of constructing a new order, the nature of self-emancipatory politics as the production of historical progress, the method of leadership conceived as fragility and experimentation, and the organisational form of the party as a pedagogical laboratory. Taken in their productive dialectical interaction, these four perspectives enable us to restore political strategy to the centre of the notion of hegemony, and offer a sophisticated perspective well placed to dialogue with some of the central concerns of contemporary radical social and political movements.
items.title: New Orders: Hegemony as a Method of Political Work

items.abstract: Against broader readings that extend reification across different social spheres, this article argues that the concept gains analytical precision when anchored in the economic fabric of society. It understands reification as arising from capitalist societalisation mediated by the commodity form. The concept designates a double form of power: first, the impersonal and abstract power generated by commodity-mediated relations; and second, the ideological power through which this historically specific order appears natural and unchangeable, fostering economic fatalism. The article also distinguishes reification from capitalist rationalisation, showing how fragmented rational calculation both presupposes and reproduces an irrational social totality. It further highlights the non-essentialist account of subjectivity on which the theory relies and clarifies the relation between reification and capitalist alienation. In doing so, it outlines a more precise framework for historicising reification and analysing its relation to socio-economic and political phenomena in contemporary capitalism.
items.title: Reification re-specified: The power of commodity-mediated societalisation

items.abstract: Dwelling is a fundamental mode of existence and a key site where contemporary societal crises manifest – from the endangered habitability of the Earth to digital exploitation and mass surveillance, from rising loneliness to the erosion of the public sphere. To grasp these phenomena, a critical theory of dwelling is needed, as the 19th-century paradigm of the bourgeois home continues to shape and amplify them. This article develops such a theory by conceptualizing dwelling as integral to processes of subjectivation, deeply embedded in specific historical, social, and technological contexts. Drawing on Walter Benjamin’s analysis of bourgeois interiors, Félix Guattari’s machinic and ecosophical thought, Michel Foucault’s investigation of space and biopower, François Béguin’s concept of the ‘domestic world’, and Paul Klee’s dialectic of home, the article critiques the hegemonic model of bourgeois dwelling and offers a framework for reimagining dwelling in light of current existential and ecological threats.
items.title: The Dwelling Question: A Critical Theory of the Bourgeois Home

items.abstract: : What is the meaning of "time" when one is "doing time'? Through a phenomenological analysis of first-person accounts, this article considers the imprint incarceration enacts upon a person's primary experience of time. This is termed carceral time, and includes experiences such as the social death of incarceration, temporal stasis, natal alienation, carceral captivity, and the foreclosing of diachronic agency. Retributivists—including Kant and Hegel—assert that punishment is justified when it is proportional to the crime. Yet, the proportionality of a prison sentence hinges on the assumption that carceral time can be calculated in terms of its equivalency or economic exchangeability to free people's experience of time. In evaluating whether incarceration is just, one must consider the impact it has on the incarcerated person. The testimonies on carceral time evince that incarceration indelibly inscribes the whole of an individual's temporal horizon and is not quantifiably proportional to ordinary 'free" experiences of time. This undermines the concept of proportional time at the heart of retributivist arguments, but also, potentially, the justness of the justice system. This artic
items.title: Carceral Time & Decarceral Time: An Account of Prison Temporality

items.abstract: : Under contemporary digital conditions, political myth operates through memes that collapse the temporal interval liberal deliberation requires. Reading the case of Luigi Mangione, I show how memetic speech acts convert resistance into spectacle, foreclosing the possibility of revolt. Drawing on theorists of myth, performativity, and revolt—from Sorel and Foucault to Barthes, Butler, and Fanon—I argue that authoritarian myths thrive on virality's affective compression, while oppositional myths are metabolized as engagement before they can mobilize rupture. The Mangione phenomenon confronts liberal complicity: when systemic violence is normalized as order, refusing counter-violence may become yet another alibi for sanctioned death.
items.title: Mythic Violence, Memes, and the Recursive Rhetorics of Resistance

items.abstract: : In On Populist Reason , Ernesto Laclau takes Freud as his point of departure to argue that populism is not a pathological form of democracy, but its intrinsic rationality and possibility, and already embedded in democratic practices, ideals, and struggles. I delineate three of Laclau's Freudian premises and identify limitations or flaws in his appropriation. In distinguishing between a primary populism and a secondary populism, I argue that both Laclau's conception of symbolic representation and his presentation of the leader's role in group psychology fall prey to a version of sovereign loyalty that undermines independent agency and judgment.
items.title: Primary Populism and Secondary Populism: Laclau, Symbolic Representation, and Group Psychology

items.abstract: : This essay explores the implications of far-Right violence for democratic theory and feminist ethics by analyzing deliberative forums and violent confrontations over Charlottesville's Confederate monuments. The forums exemplified deliberation's best participatory qualities, but failed to prevent white supremacist violence at Unite the Right. I develop the concept of Embodied Confrontation—or assembling in public space to contest attempted construction of a neo-fascist people—to theorize one radically democratic practice that remains available when far-Right violence interrupts democratic processes. Complicating feminist theories of nonviolence, I critique binary violence/nonviolence distinctions and create space for self/community defense.
items.title: Democracy & Violence in Charlottesville: Deliberation, Feminist Ethics, and Embodied Confrontation Against White Supremacy

items.abstract: : This essay includes a political repertoire for thought and action rooted in Black feminism that I call a politics of futurity . It consists of four parts: purpose, strategy, tactics, and goal. The first builds on the politics of care that I developed in Reckoning . The second adapts and extends Saidiya Hartman's method of critical fabulation augmented by a notion of political fabrication. The third suggests tactics derived from the folkloric character of the Trickster. And the fourth forwards the goal of democratic redesign and reconstruction, which we can think of as worldbuilding.
items.title: Meditations on a Politics of Futurity: A Black Feminist Repertoire for Worldbuilding

items.abstract: : This article argues that the Islamic Republic of Iran's codified and institutionalized gender apartheid created a unique form of militarized women's domestic role from which grief and mourning became protected, even expected, forms of expression for maternal subjects. Bringing Iran's unique historical and political context to bear on an analysis of bereaved mothers' affective resistance during the "Woman, Life, Freedom" (WLF) uprising, it demonstrates how mothers' expressions of "shared grief" constitute a life-affirming form of affective resistance that not only challenges sovereign erasure but also subverts traditional motherhood to perform a feminist politics of lamentation that enacts equality—revealing a maternal politics that threatens the performative undoing of Iran's essentialist gender apartheid and exposes the fragility of its theocratic rule.
items.title: Affective Resistance Against Sovereign Erasure: Historicizing the (Maternal and) Feminist Politics of Shared Grief in Iran's Woman, Life, Freedom Uprising

items.abstract: : Self-defense cases evince a primal scene of political life because they reveal the vulnerability to violence citizens may feel and highlight the power of discretionary judgment by jurors about which killings are excusable and which carry the liability of punishment by the state. This paper includes an account of a self-defense trial in La Plata, Argentina, which the author attended in May of 2024 and an interpretation of the factors, including the framework of "justifiable homicide," public distrust in the police, and empathy for the defendant, that led to the surprise acquittal.
items.title: Justice in Strife: Argentina's New Jury Trials and the Meaning of Self-Defense

items.abstract: : Drawing on ethnography, interviews, and archives, this essay charts intertwined histories of Black migrant labor, Chinese indenture, resource extraction, and race-making in the ruins of South Africa's gold mines. Connecting past to present, it examines the zama zama , informal migrant miners who work in abandoned mines, and the unmarked graves of Chinese mineworkers to understand how histories of extractive capitalism and racialized disposability reemerge, illustrating the enduring force of not only these histories but also their entanglements. It utilizes a subterranean archive of disappearing figures and buried traces and theorizes the afterlife of death.
items.title: Subterranean Traces: Unearthing Death and Disposability in the Ruins of the Mine

items.abstract: This article argues that while the instability and violence of the French Revolution has been overwhelmingly attributed to the transfer of unitary sovereignty from king to people, popular sovereignty was neither conceptually novel nor inherently destabilizing in 1789. We begin by drawing on early modern political theory, most importantly Bodin, d’Argenson and Rousseau, to argue that democracy was understood to be as much a form of government as a type of sovereignty. By tracing successive experiments from mixed government in 1789 to ‘revolutionary government’ in 1794 to imperial government under Napoleon, the article shows how suspicion towards government shaped revolutionary politics and drove institutional change. The Terror and the First Empire emerge not as inevitable outcomes of democracy, characterized by unitary popular sovereignty, but as contingent responses to perceived failures of previous governmental arrangements. By recovering a neglected history of democracy, this article renews the ambition of providing a political matrix for situating revolutionary politics within the longer historical arc of modern democratic politics.
items.title: Sovereignty and Government in the French Revolution

items.abstract: : The discussion of friendship in Eudemian Ethics VII is often taken as evidence that Aristotle relies on dialectic in this treatise. I argue that, although he uses some dialectical resources, these are insufficient for fully developing his account of friendship. His approach has four features: the arguments are philosophical, aiming at the nature and truth of friendship; he appeals to phainomena , including both endoxic and non-endoxic claims; resolving aporiai requires substantive philosophical knowledge; and, guided by epistemic optimism, he seeks to preserve what is true in existing beliefs. This contrasts with dialectical argument, which reasons from endoxic premises without aiming at endoxic conclusions.
items.journal: Journal of the History of Philosophy
items.title: Aristotle’s Nondialectical Inquiry into Friendship in the Eudemian Ethics

items.abstract: Aristotle is widely identified as foundational to the understanding of tyranny as a form of political enslavement, wherein the ruled are treated ‘like a slave’ insofar as they are subjected to the arbitrary will of another. This article challenges the collapse of Aristotelian tyranny into arbitrary rule by reconstructing what it means, on Aristotle’s understanding, for tyrants to rule ‘like a master’. Aristotle suggests that tyrants and slave masters are akin insofar as they are often driven by a longing for supremacy , a structurally embedded desire to secure a legible position of preeminent standing. The recognition of such supremacy is important for despots because it promises to vouchsafe their security from those whom they oppress. But Aristotle suggests that such desired standing is often internally unstable; oppressed actors like slaves and tyrannized citizens harbour a sense of worth or merit ( axia ) that is incompatible with the despotism of slavery or tyranny, and the repressive means through which despotic actors attempt to diminish expressions of axia among the oppressed can prove self-defeating. This article demonstrates that Aristotle’s insights into the psychologica
items.title: ‘Like a Master:’ Aristotle on Tyranny, Slavery and the Longing for Supremacy

items.abstract: : Many scholars hold that Albert the Great favors a distinction theory of the soul and its powers. According to this theory, the soul is a substance, while its powers are qualities. In this paper, I challenge this interpretation. I argue that Albert takes the soul itself to be the power to vivify the body. I also show that, for Albert, such powers as sight, which are qualities distinct from the soul, depend on this basic vivifying power. To this end, I expound Albert ’s claim that the power to vivify is “determined and specified ” by such powers as sight.
items.journal: Journal of the History of Philosophy
items.title: Albert the Great on the Soul and Its Powers

items.abstract: : This paper explores the metaphysical significance of Leibniz ’s conception of elasticity and its development during the 1680s. The first part is devoted to the discussion of elasticity as a system property in the Hypothesis physica nova of 1671. A second section shows the transition, in the second half of the 1670s, from such a conception to an understanding of elasticity as a condition for the spontaneity and individuality of bodies. Finally, through an examination of writings from the 1680s about the transmission of sound and the elastic properties of materials, I will reconstruct the underlying metaphysical framework characterizing Leibniz ’s conception of elastic matter, namely the idea of a “mechanical mirroring ” which is proper to individual bodies.
items.journal: Journal of the History of Philosophy
items.title: Leibniz’s Metaphysics of Elasticity: From the System to the Individual

items.abstract: : We provide the first in-depth analysis of Anton Wilhelm Amo ’s 1734 Tractatus de Arte Sobrie et Accurate Philosophandi by examining the fundamental role that intention plays in this work. Specifically, we argue that the “Intentional Principle, ” which states that everything that exists (except for God) is the effect of an intentional action, is key to understanding his account of the operations of human and divine spirits and his account of what exists (and why). In doing so, we demonstrate that Amo was a systematic thinker who grounded his philosophy in intention. Furthermore, we show that intentions are key to understanding Amo ’s views on what the ends of philosophy are and how philosophical inquiry ought to be pursued.
items.journal: Journal of the History of Philosophy
items.title: The Role of Intention in Anton Wilhelm Amo’s Philosophical Project

items.abstract: : This paper shows how interpreting religious scriptures contributes to applied Kantian ethics. It addresses concerns in recent literature with introducing principles of practical reason in the historical and institutional spheres. Just as the formal principles of the moral law apply under all conditions, the pure religion of reason is critically applicable to diverse historically formed religions. Interpreting traditions through pure moral religion responds to the problem of actualizing principles of practical reason in the world. For Kant, the final purpose in the interpretation of holy books is the moral improvement of human beings and the actualization of the highest good in the world.
items.journal: Journal of the History of Philosophy
items.title: Kant and the Interpretation of Religious Scriptures

items.abstract: : This paper introduces readers to a master ’s thesis defended by June Downey to the Philosophy Department of the University of Chicago in 1898. I have two goals. The first and major goal is to show that an unknown and unpublished piece of work from the end of the nineteenth century is, in fact, well worth reading. Downey ’s paper makes useful contributions to the field by foregrounding the importance of activity in Berkeley ’s metaphysics and in making a novel use of his Philosophical Commentaries . Finally, taking on board the usefulness of Downey ’s unknown work adds insights about the project of adding women to accounts of the history of philosophy.
items.journal: Journal of the History of Philosophy
items.title: June Downey’s Thesis on Berkeley on the Will

items.abstract: : In a recent issue of the Journal of the History of Philosophy , Steven Nadler draws attention to the neglected argument of François Lamy that Malebranche ’s doctrine of occasionalism conflicts with his own criticism of Descartes ’s appeal to a “force of rest ” in physics. Nadler claims that this argument is well worth considering insofar as its conclusion seems to be “absolutely correct. ” In this discussion note, I offer reasons to doubt that Lamy is in fact correct in charging that there is an internal tension on this point in Malebranche ’s system. I also briefly consider the significance of Malebranche ’s critique of Descartes for early modern Cartesian physics.
items.journal: Journal of the History of Philosophy
items.title: Lamy, Malebranche, and the Force of Rest: Reply to Nadler

items.abstract: Public debate and scholarly discussions about a crisis of institutional trust focus on an external perspective: declining citizen trust, indicating that institutions lose legitimacy. While important, this perspective does not capture a conceptually distinct and politically salient form of institutional dysfunction occurring inside institutions that can undercut their trustworthiness. We develop an internal perspective on institutional trustworthiness. It focuses on the endogenous conditions under which officeholders are warranted in trusting that their interrelated actions can uphold institutional functioning. We argue that such warranted trust is grounded in the joint realization of two commitments: (1) to mutual accountability in exercising office power and (2) to the assumption of interrelated responsibility to uphold institutional action. We call the configuration in which these commitments are jointly realized “endogenous institutional trustworthiness.” We argue that endogenous institutional trustworthiness is irreducible to standard requirements of professional ethics. It is a distinct normative standard that specifies when officeholders are warranted in trusting one another
items.title: Endogenous institutional trustworthiness
